text: La Brea is a group of pools where sticky natural asphalt, a kind of tar, oozes up from underground. For tens of thousands of years, animals walked in and couldn't get out. The tar soaked their bones and kept them safe.

Scientists have dug out millions of [[fossil|fossils]] there: Columbian [[mammoth|mammoths]], giant ground sloths, sabre-toothed cats, dire wolves, [[@camels|camels]], birds, insects and even seeds and [[pollen|pollen]]. It is one of the richest Ice Age fossil sites anywhere, and it sits beside a busy road in the [[@cities-grow|second-largest city]] in the United States.

sec.t:
Deep under Los Angeles there is oil, formed over millions of years from tiny sea creatures buried in mud. Some of it seeps up through cracks. Near the surface, the lighter parts evaporate and leave behind thick, black asphalt, the same kind of stuff used in [[@oil-coal|oil and coal]] industries and on [[@roads-built|roads]].

The name is a small joke. *La brea* means "the tar" in [[@spanish-language|Spanish]], so "the La Brea Tar Pits" means "the the tar tar pits". People living nearby used the tar long before the city existed. The Tongva people used it to waterproof baskets and seal their canoes.

When a horse or bison got stuck, it struggled and called out. Wolves and big cats came to eat it, and got stuck too. That is why La Brea has far more meat-eaters than plant-eaters. Scientists call this a [[predator|predator]] trap.

Getting stuck didn't take much. A layer of asphalt only a few centimetres deep could hold a horse, especially on a warm day when the tar was soft. Leaves and dust often hid the surface, and rainwater sometimes pooled on top, so a thirsty animal might walk in to drink.

The count is lopsided. More than 4,000 dire wolves have been found, and more than 2,000 sabre-toothed cats. In most places, plant-eaters far outnumber hunters, so La Brea gives a rare, crowded look at the [[@sabre-tooth|sabre-toothed cat]] and its rivals. The cat is now California's state fossil.

{{story:sabre-tooth}}

These animals lived during the last [[@ice-ages|Ice Age]], between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago. Los Angeles was cooler and wetter then, with woodland, grassland and streams. Many of the big animals, like the [[@mammoths|mammoths]], have since died out.

Because the pits trapped things over such a long time, scientists can compare bones from different layers. They can see how animals and plants changed as the [[climate|climate]] warmed. Scientists still argue over how much of the great die-off was caused by a changing climate and how much by the arrival of human hunters.

Among the millions of bones, only one human skeleton has been found: a woman who lived about 10,000 years ago. Museum staff call her La Brea Woman. She is a reminder that people were already living in California while mammoths still walked there.

The pits still bubble today, as gas rises through the tar and pops at the surface. In summer, fresh asphalt seeps up in lawns and car parks, and staff put up cones around it.

In 2006, builders digging an underground car park for a museum next door found 16 new fossil deposits. Rather than dig through them on the spot, workers boxed them up in wooden crates and moved them to the museum grounds. Scientists are still cleaning those crates, bone by bone, and visitors can watch through a window.

sec.t:
न्यूटन बल नापने की एक इकाई है। 100 ग्राम की चॉकलेट हाथ में पकड़े रहने के लिए लगभग 1 न्यूटन बल लगता है। एक बड़े इंसान की दाढ़ें कुछ सौ न्यूटन से दबा सकती हैं।

ज़िंदा जानवरों का दंश वैज्ञानिक सीधे नापते हैं। ग्रेगरी एरिक्सन और उनकी टीम ने गद्दी लगे बल-[[sensor|सेंसर]] मगरमच्छों और एलिगेटरों के जबड़ों के बीच पकड़े। एक बड़े खारे पानी के [[@croc-ancient|मगरमच्छ]] ने लगभग 16,000 न्यूटन से काटा। यह किसी भी ज़िंदा जीव में नापा गया सबसे ताक़तवर दंश है।

एक बड़े टी. रेक्स के लगभग 60 दाँत होते थे। सबसे लंबे दाँत, जबड़े में छिपी जड़ समेत, लगभग 30 सेंटीमीटर के हो सकते थे, मोटे तौर पर एक बड़े केले जितने। ये पतले और ब्लेड जैसे नहीं, बल्कि मोटे और गोलाई लिए हुए थे, और इनके किनारों पर आरी जैसे बारीक दाँते थे।

पतले दाँत हड्डी पर टूट जाते। मोटे दाँत अंदर घुसकर कुचल सकते थे। ज़्यादातर [[reptile|सरीसृपों]] की तरह टी. रेक्स के नए दाँत ज़िंदगी भर उगते रहते थे, इसलिए टूटा दाँत जल्दी ही बदल जाता था। तुम्हारे अपने [[@teeth|दाँत]] तो बस एक बार ही बदलते हैं।

1998 में कैरन चिन और उनके साथियों ने कनाडा के सस्कैचेवान से मिली पत्थर बन चुकी एक विशाल पॉटी के बारे में बताया। जीवाश्म बनी पॉटी को [[coprolite|कोप्रोलाइट]] कहते हैं। यह लगभग 44 सेंटीमीटर लंबी थी और पौधे खाने वाले एक छोटे डायनासोर की हड्डियों के टुकड़ों से ठसाठस भरी थी। इतनी बड़ी पॉटी सिर्फ़ टी. रेक्स ही कर सकता था।

टी. रेक्स के दाँतों के निशान वाली हड्डियाँ भी यही कहानी कहती हैं। कुछ [[@triceratops-horns|ट्राइसेराटॉप्स]] के कूल्हों और सींगों पर उसके दाँतों से बने गहरे छेद और खरोंचें हैं।

हड्डी काटने की ज़रूरत ही क्या थी? हड्डियों में खनिज और चर्बी वाला गूदा होता है, जो बड़ा पौष्टिक खाना है। आज के बहुत कम सरीसृप अपना खाना चबाते हैं। ज़्यादातर बड़े टुकड़े साबुत निगल जाते हैं। लगता है टी. रेक्स बार-बार हड्डियों को काटता था, कुछ-कुछ लकड़बग्घे या भेड़िये की तरह।

इस आदत से एक बड़ा टी. रेक्स हर [[carcass|लाश]] से ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा खाना निकाल पाता होगा, उनसे भी जिन्हें दूसरे शिकारी पहले ही नोच चुके थे।

जबड़ा एक [[@lever-lift|लीवर]] की तरह काम करता है, जिसका कब्ज़ा पीछे होता है। टी. रेक्स की खोपड़ी पीछे से चौड़ी थी, जिससे जबड़े की विशाल मांसपेशियों के लिए जगह बचती थी। उसकी खोपड़ी की हड्डियाँ भी कसकर जुड़ी हुई थीं, इसलिए काटते समय ज़्यादा मुड़ती नहीं थीं।

मोटे, नुकीले दाँतों पर लगे ताक़तवर बल से दाँतों की नोक पर ज़बरदस्त दबाव बनता था। एक अध्ययन के अनुमान के मुताबिक यह दबाव हड्डी को चूर-चूर करने लायक था, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे आज मगरमच्छ का दंश करता है।

text: Scientists think the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, extremely hot and packed tightly together. Since then it has been [[@mystery-dark-energy|expanding]] and cooling. This idea is called the Big Bang.

In the first few minutes, the simplest ingredients formed, mostly hydrogen and helium. Hundreds of millions of years later, [[gravity|gravity]] pulled that gas into the first stars and [[@galaxies|galaxies]]. Heavier [[element|elements]], like the carbon in your body and the iron in your blood, were made later inside stars.
Nobody knows what, if anything, came before. That question is still open.

myth: The Big Bang was an explosion at one spot, throwing matter out into empty space.

It wasn't an explosion in space. Space itself has been stretching everywhere at once. There is no centre where the bang happened, which is why distant galaxies are moving away from us in every direction.

sec.t:
In the 1920s, [[astronomer|astronomers]] noticed that light from distant [[galaxy|galaxies]] was stretched towards the red end of the rainbow. This "redshift" meant the galaxies were moving away from us. In 1927, a Belgian priest and physicist named Georges Lemaître suggested the universe was expanding. In 1929, the American astronomer Edwin Hubble showed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away.

Run that film backwards, and everything gets closer and closer together. Long ago, everything we can see must have been squeezed into a tiny, hot, dense state. Ideas from [[@einstein|Einstein]] about how space can stretch made the picture fit.

For its first 380,000 years or so, the universe was a glowing fog of hot gas. Light couldn't travel far before bumping into something, a bit like car headlights in thick winter fog on a Delhi highway. Then it cooled enough for the first [[atom|atoms]] to form, and the fog cleared. Light could suddenly travel freely.

The hiss that Penzias and Wilson heard is that very light, released when the fog lifted. It has been travelling for nearly 13.8 billion years, stretching all the way.

Light takes time to travel. When we see a galaxy billions of [[@light-years|light-years]] away, we see it as it was billions of years ago. [[@telescopes-how|Telescopes]] are time machines.

The James Webb Space Telescope looks for galaxies that formed in the first few hundred million years. The European Space Agency's Planck spacecraft mapped the leftover glow so precisely that scientists could pin down the universe's age to within less than one percent.

Not everyone liked the idea at first. The British astronomer Fred Hoyle argued for a "steady state" universe with no beginning, constantly making new matter. He gave the Big Bang its name on a radio programme in 1949. He later said he only wanted a vivid picture for listeners, not an insult.

The Indian astrophysicist Jayant Narlikar worked closely with Hoyle and spent much of his career exploring other ideas. Today, most scientists accept the Big Bang because so many different clues agree. Doubters played a useful part, though: questioning an idea makes everyone check the evidence harder.

sec.t:
सूरज धरती से लगभग 109 गुना चौड़ा है। इसके अंदर लगभग 13 लाख धरतियाँ समा सकती हैं। सौरमंडल के कुल द्रव्यमान का 99% से ज़्यादा हिस्सा अकेले सूरज में है, इसीलिए बुध से लेकर सबसे दूर के धूमकेतु तक, सब इसी का चक्कर लगाते हैं।

सूरज एक काफ़ी साधारण, मँझोले आकार का तारा है। यह बस इसलिए ख़ास दिखता है क्योंकि बहुत पास है। उसके बाद सबसे पास का तारा लगभग 2,70,000 गुना ज़्यादा दूर है।

सूरज की सतह लगभग 5,500 °C की है। यह गर्म गैस के उबलते खानों से ढकी है, जिनमें से हर एक लगभग 1,000 किलोमीटर चौड़ा है, महाराष्ट्र से भी ज़्यादा चौड़ा। [[@sunspots|सौर कलंक]] कहलाने वाले काले धब्बे आते-जाते रहते हैं। ये बस इसलिए काले दिखते हैं क्योंकि आसपास की गैस से थोड़े ठंडे होते हैं। सौर कलंकों की गिनती लगभग 11 साल के चक्र में घटती-बढ़ती रहती है।

कभी-कभी सूरज आवेशित गैस के विशाल बादल अंतरिक्ष में फेंक देता है। जब कोई बादल धरती से टकराता है, तो आसमान [[@aurora|ध्रुवीय ज्योति]] से जगमगा सकता है। 1859 में एक [[@space-weather|भारी सौर तूफ़ान]] की वजह से ध्रुवीय ज्योति दक्षिण में कैरिबियन तक दिखी। टेलीग्राफ़ के तारों से चिंगारियाँ निकलीं, और कुछ ऑपरेटरों ने पाया कि वे बैटरी हटाकर भी संदेश भेज पा रहे थे।

भारत का पहला सौर मिशन, आदित्य-L1, 2023 में छोड़ा गया। यह धरती से लगभग 15 लाख किलोमीटर दूर एक ऐसी जगह पर है जहाँ सूरज और धरती का खिंचाव बराबर हो जाता है, ताकि यह बिना किसी रुकावट के सूरज को देखता रहे। यह सूरज के बाहरी [[atmosphere|वायुमंडल]] और हमारी ओर भेजे जाने वाले तूफ़ानों का अध्ययन करता है।

नासा का पार्कर सोलर प्रोब उल्टी दिशा में जाता है, यानी गोता लगाकर सूरज के पास। दिसंबर 2024 में यह सतह से लगभग 60 लाख किलोमीटर दूर से गुज़रा, और इतनी तेज़ी से चला जितना इससे पहले कोई अंतरिक्ष यान नहीं चला था।

सूरज लगभग 4.6 अरब साल पुराना है, यानी अपनी ज़िंदगी के लगभग आधे रास्ते पर। लगभग 5 अरब साल बाद इसके केंद्र में हाइड्रोजन कम पड़ने लगेगी, और यह फूलकर एक [[@star-life-cycle|लाल दानव]] बन जाएगा। तब तक इसकी रोशनी लगभग हर जीव का पेट भरती है, उन पौधों के ज़रिए जो इसे [[@photosynthesis|प्रकाश-संश्लेषण]] में पकड़ते हैं। और हमारी बिजली का बढ़ता हिस्सा [[@solar-panels|सोलर पैनलों]] से आ रहा है।

text: A helicopter flies because its long, thin rotor blades are wings. Instead of the whole aircraft rushing forward to move air over its wings, like a plane, a helicopter spins its wings round and round. Each blade is shaped and tilted to push air downwards, and the air pushes the blade up. That push is called [[lift|lift]].

Spin the blades fast enough and the lift becomes greater than the helicopter's weight, so it rises. That's why a helicopter can take off straight up, hover in one place and land on a rooftop, a ship or a mountainside, places no plane could reach.

st.prompt: What would happen to a helicopter with a big top rotor but no tail rotor?

options.t: Its body would spin round the opposite way to the blades
Nothing, the tail rotor is just for steering left and right

st.reveal: Spinning the big rotor one way pushes the body the other way. The small tail rotor pushes sideways to cancel that out. Helicopters with two big rotors spinning in opposite directions, like the Chinook, don't need one.

myth: If a helicopter's engine stops, it falls like a stone.
Pilots train for this. They tilt the blades so the air rushing up through them keeps them spinning, like a sycamore seed. This is called autorotation, and it lets the helicopter glide down and land.

sec.t:
The pilot has two main controls for the blades. One, the collective, changes the angle of all the blades at once. More angle means more lift, so the helicopter rises. Less angle and it sinks.

The other, the cyclic, tilts the spinning disc of blades slightly, so it pushes air down and a little backwards. The helicopter then moves forwards. Tilt it to the side, and it slides sideways. It is a bit like tilting an umbrella in a strong wind. The whole aircraft follows the direction of the tilt.

Children in China played with spinning bamboo toys, the bamboo-copter, more than 1,500 years ago. Around 1490, [[@leonardo|Leonardo da Vinci]] sketched an "aerial screw", a spiral sail meant to twist its way into the sky. It could never have flown, but the idea was there.

Real helicopters were very hard to build. Early machines shook, spun and tipped over. In 1939, the Russian-American engineer Igor Sikorsky flew the VS-300 in Connecticut, USA. It had one main rotor and a small tail rotor, the design most helicopters still use today.

Helicopters go where planes can't. They lift sick people from accident sites, pluck sailors off sinking ships and [[@people-firefighters-forest|fight forest fires]] with giant buckets of water.

In June 2013, [[@floods-why|floods]] and [[@landslides|landslides]] struck [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], around Kedarnath. Indian Air Force helicopters flew hundreds of trips through narrow mountain valleys and helped [[@people-mountain-rescuers|rescue many thousands of people]]. India builds its own helicopters too. The HAL Dhruv, designed and made by Hindustan Aeronautics in Bengaluru, first flew in 1992.

Thin air is hard for helicopters, because the blades have less air to push. In May 2005, French test pilot Didier Delsalle landed a specially prepared helicopter on the summit of [[@everest-first|Mount Everest]], 8,848 m up, a record that still stands.

In 2021, a helicopter flew somewhere even stranger. NASA's tiny Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet, on Mars, where the air is about a hundredth as thick as Earth's. The same idea, smaller and with four rotors, now lifts the [[@drones|drones]] you see over weddings and cricket grounds.

text: When the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] sweeps across India in June and July, it brings some birds with it, and it sends many others into a frenzy of nest-building.

The most famous [[monsoon|monsoon]] messenger is the pied cuckoo, a black-and-white bird with a crest. In much of north and central India, it appears around the time the rains arrive, and its loud, ringing calls are taken as a sign that the monsoon is near. The Indian pitta, a small, very colourful bird, also arrives in many forests to breed.
Many birds that live in India all year, such as baya weavers, storks and sarus cranes, time their breeding for the rainy months, when food is everywhere.

sec.t:
The pied cuckoo, also called the Jacobin cuckoo, is known in Hindi and many other languages as the chatak or chataka. In Indian [[@poetry|poetry]] and songs, the chatak waits for the first drops of rain and drinks nothing else. It became a symbol of longing and patient waiting.

[[biologist|Biologists]] see a different story. Some pied cuckoos live in south India all year. Others appear in north India just before or with the monsoon, then leave once it ends. Many scientists think these northern birds fly in from eastern Africa, crossing the Arabian Sea on the monsoon winds, but the details are still being worked out.

Like many cuckoos, it never raises its own family. It lays its eggs in the nests of babblers, noisy brown birds that bring up the cuckoo chicks as if they were their own.

The rains turn many resident birds into builders. Baya weavers, small yellow-and-brown birds, weave hanging nests from long strips of grass, often over water. The male builds the nest. Females inspect it, and if one approves, the male finishes it. The finished nest, with a long entrance tube pointing straight down, is one of the most skilful [[@bird-nests|bird nests]] in India.

In grasslands of central and western India, the male lesser florican, a rare bustard, leaps high above the grass again and again in the monsoon to attract a mate. Asian openbill storks and egrets gather to nest in trees beside flooded fields.

All this activity runs on food. Rain makes [[@insects-importance|insects]] hatch in huge numbers, and ponds fill with frogs, snails and fish.

Some of the most dramatic arrivals come as the monsoon ends. In October and November, huge flocks of Amur falcons stop in Nagaland, in [[@northeast-india|northeast India]], to feed on flying termites. They are on one of the longest migrations of any bird of prey, from eastern Asia to southern Africa.

Around 2012, many of the falcons were being trapped for food. Conservation groups worked with village communities in Nagaland, and hunting fell sharply. Today, villages such as Pangti welcome [[@birdwatching|birdwatchers]] instead, and the falcons' return has become a celebration. Soon after, winter visitors like ducks and cranes begin arriving from Central Asia and Siberia, as India's bird calendar turns once again.

text: At least two kinds of birds are known to sleep while flying. The first is the frigatebird, a big seabird with long, thin wings. In 2016, scientists fitted frigatebirds with tiny brain recorders and proved they nap in mid-air, often with only one half of the brain asleep at a time.

The second is the swift. Swifts are small, sleek birds that live almost entirely in the air. Some common swifts stay aloft for about ten months without landing, so they must sleep while flying, though nobody has yet recorded their brains to prove it. Their look-alikes, the swallows, are less extreme. They spend hours flying but come down to perch and sleep.

sec.t:
Common swifts breed in Europe and parts of Asia and spend the northern winter over Africa. For years, people suspected they rarely landed. In 2016, a team at Lund University in Sweden fixed tiny data loggers, weighing about as much as a paperclip, to swifts' backs.

When the birds returned the next year, the loggers showed that some had flown non-stop for about ten months, all the way to Africa and back. They caught insects in the air and probably drank by skimming raindrops or water surfaces.

At dusk, swifts often climb high into the sky, up to a few kilometres. Scientists think they glide slowly down from there, snatching short naps on the way. A young swift that leaves its nest may not touch the ground again until it is ready to breed, perhaps two years later.

Frigatebirds soar over [[tropical|tropical]] oceans for weeks, hunting fish and squid. They can't land on the water because their feathers aren't waterproof.

In 2016, scientists led by Niels Rattenborg recorded the brain waves of great frigatebirds flying over the Pacific near the Galápagos Islands. The birds slept for only seconds at a time, mostly while gliding upward on rising warm air. Often, one half of the brain slept while the other stayed awake, with one eye open, looking ahead. On land, they slept for around 12 hours a day. In the air, they managed under an hour.

[[@dolphins-click|Dolphins]] do something similar, resting half their brain at a time so they can keep swimming and breathing.

{{story:sleep-why}}

Swifts and swallows both have long, pointed wings, short beaks and wide mouths for scooping up insects. But they're not closely related. Swifts belong to the same group as hummingbirds. Swallows are songbirds, related to sparrows.

You can tell them apart by watching them land. Swifts have tiny legs and feet that are good for clinging to walls and cliffs but useless for walking or perching. Their family name means "without feet". Swallows have proper perching feet and often line up on electricity wires.

Barn swallows nest in both India and the USA, gluing cup-shaped nests of mud under bridges and roofs. Many [[migration|migrate]] thousands of kilometres each year.

Swifts and their relatives make unusual homes. Many glue their [[@bird-nests|nests]] together with sticky [[saliva|saliva]]. India's Asian palm swift sticks its nest, and even its eggs, to the underside of a palm leaf, so they stay put as the leaf swings in the wind.

Edible-nest swiftlets build nests almost entirely of hardened saliva, deep in dark caves. Some find their way in the dark using clicking sounds, a simple form of [[echolocation|echolocation]]. Their nests are collected for bird's nest soup, an expensive dish in East Asia. In the [[@andaman|Andaman]] Islands, over-collection badly hurt these birds, and conservationists have worked with local people to protect nests and let chicks fly.

text: हाँ। लगभग 5 करोड़ साल पहले चार टाँगों वाले कुछ छोटे [[mammal|स्तनधारी]] खाना ढूँढने और ख़तरे से छिपने के लिए पानी में उतरने लगे। करोड़ों सालों में उनके [[descendant|वंशज]] तैरने में और माहिर होते गए। उनकी अगली टाँगें फ़्लिपर बन गईं, पिछली टाँगें सिकुड़कर ग़ायब हो गईं, और पूँछ पर चपटे पंख उग आए।
यही जानवर आज की व्हेल और डॉल्फ़िन बने। व्हेल आज भी हवा में साँस लेती हैं और दूसरे स्तनधारियों की तरह अपने बच्चों को दूध पिलाती हैं।
कुछ सबसे ज़रूरी सुराग भारत से मिले हैं। व्हेल का एक अहम रिश्तेदार, इंडोहायस, जम्मू और कश्मीर में मिला। इसकी हड्डियाँ भारतीय [[geologist|भूवैज्ञानिक]] ए. रंगा राव ने इकट्ठा की थीं।

sec.t:
व्हेल के कान में एक अनोखी हड्डी होती है, मोटी और भारी, जिसका किनारा मुड़ा हुआ होता है। किसी और स्तनधारी में ठीक ऐसी हड्डी नहीं होती। इसलिए जब वैज्ञानिकों को ज़मीनी जानवरों के [[fossil|जीवाश्मों]] में ठीक ऐसी ही कान की हड्डी मिली, तो वे समझ गए कि उन्हें व्हेल के शुरुआती रिश्तेदार मिल गए हैं।

सबसे पहला था पाकिसीटस, भेड़िये के आकार का एक जानवर, जो 1980 के दशक की शुरुआत में पाकिस्तान में मिला। फिर आया इंडोहायस। रंगा राव ने इसके जीवाश्म दशकों पहले कालाकोट के पास इकट्ठा किए थे। उनके निधन के बाद उनके परिवार ने ये पत्थर अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक हान्स थ्यूइसन को दे दिए। थ्यूइसन के मुताबिक प्रयोगशाला के एक कर्मचारी से ग़लती से एक खोपड़ी टूटकर खुल गई, और अंदर वही पहचानी हुई कान की हड्डी थी।

इंडोहायस लगभग एक बड़ी बिल्ली जितना था और कुछ-कुछ नन्हे हिरण जैसा दिखता था। उसकी हड्डियाँ दरियाई घोड़े की तरह मोटी और भारी थीं, जो पानी में चलते समय उसे नीचे टिके रहने में मदद करती होंगी।

शुरुआती व्हेलों के कई अहम जीवाश्म भारत और पाकिस्तान से आए हैं। वजह यह है कि उस ज़माने में यह इलाका टेथिस नाम के एक गर्म, उथले समुद्र का तट था। जैसे-जैसे भारत उत्तर की ओर खिसककर एशिया से टकराया, जैसा [[@india-drift|भारत के सफ़र]] में बताया गया है, वह समुद्र बंद हो गया और उसका तल उठकर जीवाश्मों से भरी पहाड़ियाँ बन गया।

गुजरात के कच्छ में भारतीय [[paleontologist|जीवाश्म विज्ञानी]] सुनील बाजपेयी और उनके साथियों को और भी शुरुआती व्हेलें मिली हैं। इनमें ऊदबिलाव जैसी एक छोटी व्हेल भी है, जिसका नाम कच्छीसीटस रखा गया।

sec.h: अजीब जगहों पर व्हेल की हड्डियाँ
sec.t:
1830 के दशक में अमेरिका के लुइज़ियाना और अलाबामा के खेतों में विशाल हड्डियाँ निकलीं। एक वैज्ञानिक को लगा कि ये किसी विशाल [[@ocean-reptiles|समुद्री सरीसृप]] की हैं, और उसने इसका नाम बेसिलोसॉरस रखा, यानी "छिपकलियों का राजा"। बाद में पता चला कि यह व्हेल थी। आज यह अलाबामा राज्य का आधिकारिक जीवाश्म है।

मिस्र के रेगिस्तान में वादी अल-हितान, यानी "व्हेलों की घाटी", बेसिलोसॉरस के कंकालों से पटी पड़ी है। कुछ कंकालों में उनकी नन्ही टाँगें अब भी अपनी जगह पर हैं। अब यह [[@unesco-sites|यूनेस्को के विश्व धरोहर स्थलों]] में से एक है।

आज की व्हेलें भी अपने अतीत के निशान लिए घूमती हैं। कई व्हेलों के शरीर में कूल्हे की छोटी हड्डियाँ दबी होती हैं। व्हेल के भ्रूण में कुछ समय के लिए वहाँ छोटे उभार उगते हैं जहाँ पिछली टाँगें होतीं। 2006 में जापान के मछुआरों ने तो एक ऐसी डॉल्फ़िन पकड़ी, जिसकी पूँछ के पास छोटे पंखों की एक अतिरिक्त जोड़ी थी, ठीक उस जगह जहाँ कभी पिछली टाँगें उगती थीं। उसकी चचेरी बहनें, जैसे [[@blue-whale|नीली व्हेल]], पानी में उतरने वाले उन पहले जानवरों से बहुत लंबा सफ़र तय कर चुकी हैं।

text: Blackbucks are fast because they [[evolve|evolved]] on open grasslands, where there was nowhere to hide. On flat plains, the best defence against wolves, and long ago against cheetahs, was to see danger early and outrun it. Over countless generations, the quickest blackbucks survived and passed on their long, slim legs and light bodies.

A blackbuck can reach about 80 km/h in short bursts and keep up a fast pace for longer than most [[predator|predators]]. It is one of the fastest land animals in India. Only a few antelope in Africa, and the cheetah, run much faster.

sec.t:
A blackbuck is light, weighing about 20 to 57 kg as an adult male, roughly as much as a teenage child. Its legs are thin and long, with most of the muscle packed high up near the body. That keeps the lower legs light, so they can swing back and forth very quickly, like a [[pendulum|pendulum]].

Big eyes on the sides of the head give the blackbuck a wide view of the plains. It can spot movement across a field while still grazing. Herds keep watch together, and when one animal bolts, the rest follow at once.

Blackbucks once roamed in huge herds across India's plains. Hunting and the loss of grasslands to farms made them disappear from much of the country. Today they live mostly in protected areas and in places where local people guard them.

The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan is famous for protecting blackbucks and chinkara. Their faith forbids harming animals and green trees. In 1730, in the village of Khejarli, many Bishnoi people are said to have given their lives to stop trees being cut, a story that later inspired the [[@chipko|Chipko movement]]. Today Bishnoi families still rush injured blackbucks to rescue centres. Blackbuck hunting is illegal in India, and well-known cases have ended up in court.

Some of the best places to see blackbucks are Velavadar National Park in Gujarat and Tal Chhapar in Rajasthan. The blackbuck is the state animal of Punjab, Haryana and Andhra Pradesh. Thanks to protection, its numbers have grown, and the IUCN now lists it as Least Concern.

In the 1930s, ranchers took blackbucks to Texas in the USA. They thrived on the dry grasslands there, and many thousands now live on ranches across the state. Argentina has a wild population too. So an Indian antelope now races across American and South American plains. Long ago, the blackbuck's main hunter in India was the Asiatic cheetah, which vanished from the country by the 1950s. Now that India has brought [[@cheetah-return|cheetahs back]] from Africa, the old race between the two could return. Both are built for [[@grasslands|open grasslands]], and both need them.

text: A phone screen is a sandwich of very thin layers. On top is a sheet of toughened [[@glass-made|glass]]. Under it sits a touch layer that senses your fingers. Below that is the display itself, made of millions of tiny dots called [[@pixels|pixels]], each built from red, green and blue parts that light up in different mixes. At the bottom is a layer of tiny electronic switches that tell each [[pixel|pixel]] what to do.

These layers are made in spotless factories called cleanrooms, mostly in South Korea, China, Japan and Taiwan. Machines lay down materials thinner than a hair, one layer at a time, on huge glass sheets that are later cut into many screens.

sec.t:
The cover glass on many phones is made by a method called fusion draw. Melted glass overflows from both sides of a long trough, like water spilling over a bathtub. The two streams meet underneath and fuse into one sheet, which is pulled down and cools. Because the surface never touches a roller, it comes out smooth and flat without polishing.

Then the glass is strengthened. Cut pieces are dipped in a bath of molten potassium salt at about 400 °C. Large potassium [[atom|atoms]] push into the surface and take the place of smaller sodium atoms. Crammed in, they squeeze the surface tight, so small cracks find it much harder to spread.

Screens are built in factories far cleaner than a hospital operating theatre. Workers wear suits that cover everything but their eyes. A single speck of dust could create a dead pixel.

Screens start on enormous sheets of glass, some of them bigger than a car parking space. Machines lay down a layer of tiny electronic switches called thin-film [[transistor|transistors]], one or more for every sub-pixel. For OLED screens, the glowing materials are heated in a [[vacuum|vacuum]] so they turn into vapour and settle through a metal stencil with millions of tiny holes. Afterwards, the sheet is sealed, tested and cut into dozens of phone-sized screens.

sec.h: How the screen feels your finger
sec.t:
Above the display is a [[@touchscreens|touchscreen]] layer. It is a grid of see-through lines made from indium tin oxide, a material that conducts electricity yet lets light pass. The grid holds a small electric field.

Your skin conducts electricity. When your finger comes close, it disturbs the field at that spot. A tiny chip checks the grid many times a second and works out exactly where you touched, even with several fingers at once.

Folding phones need a screen that can bend thousands of times. Their top layer is a tough plastic film or glass so thin, sometimes around 30 micrometres, that it flexes like paper. The OLED layers underneath have no backlight, which helps them bend.

All of this has to be assembled, tested and fitted into a phone. And the strangest part? The switches behind every pixel are made with the same kind of technology as computer chips, which is why countries like India are now racing to build [[@semiconductors-india|chip factories]] of their own.

text: When a car crashes, it stops almost instantly. The people inside don't. They keep moving forward at the speed the car was going, until something stops them. Without a belt, that something might be the steering wheel, the windscreen or the seat in front.

A seatbelt stops you along with the car. It holds you across your hips and chest, which are protected by strong [[@bones|bones]], and spreads the force over a wide area. The belt also stretches very slightly, so you slow down a fraction more gently.
That's why a seatbelt is one of the simplest, cheapest safety devices ever made, and one of the most effective. In the USA, safety experts estimate belts save around 15,000 lives a year.

sec.t:
Early seatbelts were simple straps across the lap. They helped, but in a crash the body could fold forward over them, injuring the stomach and head. In 1959, an engineer named Nils Bohlin, working at the Swedish carmaker Volvo, designed a better belt. It had one strap over the shoulder and one across the hips, joining at a buckle beside the seat. This is the three-point belt that almost every car uses today.

Volvo patented it, then did something unusual. It let any carmaker use the design for free, because it was too important to keep for itself. Safety researchers estimate the three-point belt has saved more than a million lives worldwide.

A seatbelt has to let you move normally but lock instantly in a crash. Inside the reel by your shoulder is a spring that keeps the belt snug, and a locking mechanism. A small weight or a spinning catch reacts to a sudden jerk or a sharp stop, and jams the reel so no more belt can come out.

Many modern cars go further. [[sensor|Sensors]] trigger tiny charges called pretensioners that pull the belt tight in the first instant of a crash. Others have load limiters that let the belt give a little, so it doesn't press too hard on the chest. Belts are designed to work with [[@airbags|airbags]], not instead of them.

Many people buckle up in front and forget in the back. In India, the law has long required belts in all seats, but for years few people wore them in the back. In 2022, after a well-known businessman died in a crash while riding in the back seat without a belt, the issue became front-page news and police started enforcing the rule more often.

Back-seat passengers without belts are at serious risk themselves. They can also be thrown forward into the people in front. Children need car seats or booster seats until they're big enough for an adult belt to fit across their hips and shoulder, not their stomach and neck.

text: बाउल पूर्वी भारत और बांग्लादेश के बंगाल के घुमंतू गायक और साधक हैं। वे गाँव-गाँव घूमते हैं और प्रेम, ईश्वर और ज़िंदगी के मतलब के गीत गाते हैं, अक्सर बदले में खाना या छोटे-मोटे तोहफ़े पाकर। बहुत-से बाउल केसरिया या पैबंद लगे रंग-बिरंगे ढीले चोगे पहनते हैं और लंबे बाल रखते हैं।

बाउल आम तौर पर इकतारा बजाता है, जो लौकी और चिरे हुए बाँस से बना एक तार वाला बाजा है। कई बाउल टखनों पर घुँघरू बाँधकर गाते हुए नाचते भी हैं। उनके गीत कहते हैं कि ईश्वर मंदिरों, मस्जिदों या पवित्र [[scripture|ग्रंथों]] में नहीं, हर इंसान के भीतर मिलता है। इस भीतरी दिव्य उपस्थिति को वे *मनेर मानुष* कहते हैं, यानी "मन का मानुष"। 2008 में यूनेस्को ने बाउल गीतों को दुनिया की अमूर्त सांस्कृतिक विरासत की सूची में जोड़ा।

sec.t:
बाउल हिंदू और मुसलमान, दोनों तरह के परिवारों से आते हैं, और कुछ का इस परंपरा से कोई पारिवारिक नाता ही नहीं होता। बहुत-से लोग गाँव की आम ज़िंदगी छोड़कर किसी गुरु के पीछे चल पड़ते हैं, और उनके साथ रहकर गीत और साधना सीखते हैं।

वे वैष्णव हिंदू धर्म, बौद्ध परंपराओं और सूफ़ी इस्लाम के विचारों को मिलाते हैं, और [[@caste-history|जाति]] को नकारते हैं। *बाउल* शब्द शायद संस्कृत के किसी ऐसे शब्द से आया है जिसका मतलब है "पागल" या "बेचैन", क्योंकि कहा जाता है कि बाउल ईश्वर के प्रेम में बावरे होते हैं। पक्का कोई नहीं जानता।

कवि [[@tagore|रवींद्रनाथ टैगोर]] ने ग्रामीण बंगाल में अपने परिवार की जागीरों पर बाउल गीत सुनते हुए बचपन बिताया। उन्होंने इन गीतों को इकट्ठा किया, इन पर लिखा और अपने काम में इनका सीधा, असरदार अंदाज़ अपनाया। उनके कुछ सबसे चहेते गीत बाउल धुनों पर हैं।

सबसे साफ़ मिसाल है "आमार सोनार बांग्ला", जिसे टैगोर ने 1905 में लिखा। इसकी धुन गगन हरकरा के एक बाउल गीत पर आधारित है, जो गाँव के डाकिये थे। 1971 में यह गीत बांग्लादेश का राष्ट्रगान बना। यानी जब भी वह [[@anthems|राष्ट्रगान]] बजता है, एक बाउल की धुन सुनाई देती है।

इकतारे के अलावा बाउल दोतारा बजाते हैं, जो कई तारों वाला लंबी गर्दन का बाजा है, और डुबकी या डुग्गी नाम का छोटा ढोल। खमक, या आनंदलहरी, एक छोटा ढोल है जिससे एक तार जुड़ा होता है। बजाने वाला तार को कसता-ढीला करता है, जिससे एक टनटनाती, बोलती-सी आवाज़ निकलती है।

इकतारा खुद सीधा है पर चतुराई से बना है। उसकी बाँस की दो भुजाओं को दबाने से तार का खिंचाव बदलता है, और उसके साथ सुर की [[pitch|ऊँचाई]] भी, क्योंकि तार की [[vibration|कंपन]] की रफ़्तार बदल जाती है।

1960 के दशक में बाउल गायक पूर्णदास बाउल अमेरिका गए और वहाँ के संगीतकारों से मिले। बॉब डिलन के 1967 के एल्बम *जॉन वेस्ली हार्डिंग* के कवर पर उनके साथ दो बाउल दिखते हैं। पूर्णदास बाउल दशकों तक दुनिया भर में गाते रहे।

आज सबसे बड़ा जमावड़ा पश्चिम बंगाल के बीरभूम में जयदेव केंदुली का मेला है, जो हर जनवरी में मकर संक्रांति के आसपास लगता है। हज़ारों बाउल आते हैं, डेरे डालते हैं और अजय नदी के किनारे दिन-रात गाते हैं। कुछ लोगों को फ़िक्र है कि बाउल संगीत सैलानियों के लिए तमाशा बनता जा रहा है, जबकि दूसरे कहते हैं कि नए श्रोता इसे ज़िंदा रखने में मदद करते हैं।

text: भूपेन खख्खर एक भारतीय चित्रकार थे, जिनका जन्म 1934 में [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] में हुआ। वे आम ज़िंदगी के रंग-बिरंगे, चुटीले चित्रों के लिए मशहूर हुए। उन्होंने नाई, दर्ज़ी, घड़ीसाज़ और मिठाई खाते आदमी बनाए, यानी वे लोग जिन्हें उनके ज़माने के ज़्यादातर कलाकार नज़रअंदाज़ कर देते थे।

sec.t:
खख्खर बंबई के एक गुजराती परिवार में पले-बढ़े। उन्होंने कॉमर्स, यानी व्यापार और [[economy|अर्थव्यवस्था]] से जुड़ी पढ़ाई की और चार्टर्ड अकाउंटेंट बने, यानी ऐसा काम जिसमें कंपनियों के हिसाब-किताब और टैक्स की जाँच होती है।

पर कला उन्हें अपनी ओर खींचती रही। 1950 के दशक के आखिर में वे चित्रकार और कवि ग़ुलाम मोहम्मद शेख़ से मिले, जिन्होंने उन्हें बड़ौदा आने का हौसला दिया। वहाँ 1960 के दशक की शुरुआत में खख्खर ने शहर के मशहूर ललित कला संकाय में कला-आलोचना पढ़ी। उन्होंने खुद चित्र बनाना सीखा, अक्सर देर रात तक काम करते हुए, और बरसों तक आधे समय की अकाउंटेंसी की नौकरी करते रहे। दोनों दुनियाएँ एक-दूसरे को खुराक देती रहीं। काम की वजह से वे उन दफ़्तरों, दुकानों और गलियों को जानते थे जहाँ आम लोग अपने दिन बिताते हैं, और वही उनके चित्रों के विषय बन गए।

1980 के दशक में खख्खर के चित्र ज़्यादा निजी हो गए। वे अपनी भावनाएँ खुलकर दिखाने लगे, जिनमें मर्दों के बीच का प्यार भी था। उस समय भारत में ऐसे रिश्ते कानून के ख़िलाफ़ थे। 1981 का एक चित्र, *यू कांट प्लीज़ ऑल*, यानी "सबको खुश नहीं रखा जा सकता", एक आदमी को बालकनी पर खड़े होकर नीचे खेली जा रही एक पुरानी [[fable|लोककथा]] को देखते हुए दिखाता है। बहुत-से आलोचक इसे खख्खर का दुनिया से यह कहना मानते हैं कि वे जैसे हैं, वैसे ही जिएँगे और चित्र बनाएँगे।

कुछ लोग हैरान हुए। दूसरों ने उनकी हिम्मत की तारीफ़ की। उनकी मृत्यु के पंद्रह साल बाद, 2018 में, भारत के सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने समलैंगिक रिश्तों के ख़िलाफ़ कानून खत्म कर दिया, और बहुत-से लेखक आज खख्खर को [[@equality|बराबरी]] की एक शुरुआती, शांत आवाज़ के रूप में याद करते हैं।

खख्खर ने गुजराती में कहानियाँ और नाटक भी लिखे, अक्सर मज़ेदार और हल्के व्यंग्य वाले। वे मिलनसार इंसान थे, भारत और ब्रिटेन के कलाकारों और लेखकों में उनके दोस्त थे, और 1970 के दशक से वे यूरोप में नियमित रूप से प्रदर्शनियाँ करते रहे।

आखिरी सालों में वे कैंसर से बीमार हुए और उन्होंने जल-रंगों में अपने शरीर और अपने डरों के चित्र बनाए, उसी बेबाकी के साथ। भारत ने उन्हें 1984 में पद्मश्री दिया, और नीदरलैंड ने 2000 में प्रिंस क्लॉस पुरस्कार।

2016 में [[@london|लंदन]] के टेट मॉडर्न ने उनके काम की एक बड़ी प्रदर्शनी लगाई, जिसका नाम उनके मशहूर चित्र पर था। भारतीय कला के बारे में कम जानने वाले लोग भी आधी सदी पहले बड़ौदा में बनाए गए नाइयों, दर्ज़ियों और जलेबी खाने वालों को देखकर मुस्कुराने लगे। [[@sh-raza|एस.एच. रज़ा]] और [[@mf-husain|एम.एफ़. हुसैन]] जैसे चित्रकारों के साथ मिलकर उन्होंने भारतीय आधुनिक कला को उसकी बहुत-सी अलग-अलग आवाज़ें देने में मदद की थी।

text: Democracy is a way of running a country where the people choose who governs them, and can replace those leaders at the next election. Power comes from the voters, not from a king, an army or one family.

The word is Greek. *Demos* means "the people" and *kratos* means "rule", so democracy means "rule by the people". Today most countries call themselves democracies, though some hold elections that are not really free. A working democracy needs more than voting. It needs fair rules, a free press, courts that are independent, and the freedom to disagree without being punished.

sec.h: Two ways to rule by the people
sec.t:
In a direct democracy, citizens vote on the laws themselves. That works in a small place. In the Swiss cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, voters still meet in an open-air square once a year and decide by a show of hands.

A country of crores of people cannot fit into one square. So most democracies are representative: you elect someone to make laws on your behalf, and if you dislike what they do, you vote for someone else next time. India's MPs and America's members of Congress are representatives. Some countries mix both ways and hold a [[referendum|referendum]], a direct public vote on a single question.

Early modern democracies were not open to everyone either. In the United States, women won the vote nationally only in 1920, and many Black Americans in the South were kept from voting until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

India made a bold choice. Its [[@constitution|Constitution]] gave every adult the vote from the very start, whatever their religion, caste, wealth or gender. In the first general election of 1951–52, most voters could not read, so each party had a picture symbol on the [[@election-commission|ballot]]. Indian ballots still carry symbols today.

In 1863, during the American Civil War, President [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] described democracy as "government of the people, by the people, for the people". The phrase from his Gettysburg Address is still quoted around the world.

India is the largest democracy on Earth. In 2024, about 97 crore people were registered to [[@vote-how|vote]], more than the entire population of Europe. The United States has one of the oldest written national [[constitution|constitutions]] still in use, from 1789. The two countries elect their leaders in very different ways, but both rest on the same promise: the people in power must ask the rest of us for permission, again and again.

Democracy can be slow and noisy. People argue, parties compete and decisions take time. Supporters say that is the point. Arguing in public lets mistakes be spotted, and elections let a country change direction without anyone fighting in the streets. Many thinkers have pointed out that a democracy lasts only as long as its citizens keep taking part.

text: The most common way is to set a poverty line: the smallest amount of money a person needs each day for food and other basics. Anyone living on less is counted as poor.

To find out how many people are below the line, governments run big [[@surveys|surveys]] that ask lakhs of families what they spend. Some measures also check whether people have things like schooling, clean water and electricity.

quiz.prompt: Why do experts adjust money for local prices when comparing poverty between countries?

options.t: The same amount of money buys different amounts in different countries
Prices are exactly the same everywhere

quiz.reveal: A plate of rice and dal costs far less in a small Indian town than in New York. If you simply swapped rupees into dollars, people in India would look poorer than they really are. So experts use purchasing power parity, which compares what money can actually buy.

news.h: World Bank says India lifted 496 million people out of poverty in 12 years
news.t: On 30 October 2026, news outlets reported the World Bank's latest Poverty and Equity Brief for India. It said extreme poverty, living on under $3 a day, fell from 27.1% to 2.6% between 2011-12 and 2023-24, and about 496 million people moved above the $4.20-a-day line. The report also warned that some gains may partly reflect better measurement.

d.try: With a grown-up, list what your family spends in a day on food, travel and other needs. Divide by the number of people at home. That is your daily spending per person, the same number poverty surveys try to measure for millions of families.
myth: Poverty just means not having much money.

Money matters, but so do clean water, a toilet, electricity, schooling and healthcare. That is why many experts also use multidimensional measures that check what people can actually get and do, not just what they spend.

Multidimensional poverty looks at health, education and living standards

sec.t:
A poverty line usually starts with food: how much it costs to eat enough food, with enough [[nutrition|nutrition]], to stay healthy. Then it adds other needs, such as clothes, rent and travel.

The World Bank sets a global line so countries can be compared. Its extreme poverty line is $3.00 a day per person, and a higher line of $4.20 a day is used for countries like India. These are not ordinary dollars. They are adjusted for local prices using purchasing power parity, because a rupee goes further in a village than a dollar does in a big American city.

Prices change too. With [[@inflation|inflation]], the same line must be updated every few years.

Some measures go beyond spending. Multidimensional poverty asks about health, education and living standards: Does anyone in the family go hungry? Are the children in school? Is there a toilet, clean water, electricity and cooking gas?

These measures show where help is most needed, from cities to [[@villages-india|villages]]. In October 2026, the [[@world-bank-imf|World Bank]] said India's extreme poverty had fallen from 27.1% to 2.6% between 2011-12 and 2023-24, while noting that better surveys may explain part of the change. Experts still debate exact numbers, but they agree that how you measure shapes what you see.

text: National symbols are pictures, animals, plants and songs that a country picks to stand for itself. They appear on coins, passports, government buildings and school textbooks, and they help people feel they belong to one nation.

India's main official symbols include the national flag and the national emblem, the Lion Capital of Ashoka. There is also a national anthem, a national song and a national calendar, and animals such as the tiger and the peacock. Each was chosen for a reason, and most have long roots in Indian history and nature.

st.prompt: Which of these is officially India's national game?

st.reveal: Many textbooks once said hockey, because of India's Olympic success. But in 2012, the Sports Ministry said in reply to a public question that no sport had ever been officially declared the national game.

It is widely believed, and hockey has a proud history in India. But the government has said no sport has been officially declared the national game.

sec.t:
The tiger became the national animal in 1973, the year India launched Project Tiger to save the big cats from vanishing. It replaced the lion, which had held the title before. You can find out why every tiger's coat is different in [[@tiger-stripes|tiger stripes]].

The Indian peafowl, usually called the [[@peacock-tail|peacock]], became the national bird in 1963. It is protected by law. In 2009, the Ganges river dolphin, a nearly blind dolphin that finds food by sound, was named the national aquatic animal. The elephant was declared the national heritage animal in 2010.

The lotus is widely recognised as the national flower, and the banyan as the national tree, with its roots dropping from branches to form new trunks.

*Jana Gana Mana*, written by Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]], is the national anthem. *Vande Mataram*, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and published in his 1882 novel *Anandamath*, is the national song and was a rallying cry of the freedom movement. Both have equal honour.

In 1957, India also adopted a national calendar based on the Saka era. Government gazettes and All India Radio use its dates alongside the usual Gregorian ones.

sec.h: A new symbol for the rupee
sec.t: In 2010, India chose a symbol for [[@life-money-world|its currency]], ₹, after a public competition. It was designed by D. Udaya Kumar and blends the Devanagari letter "ra" with the Roman letter "R". A line across the top echoes the flag.

Some things on popular lists are not official at all. The best-known example is the claim that [[@hockey-india|hockey]] is the national game. India's eight Olympic [[@dhyan-chand|hockey]] gold medals made it feel like one, but the government has said no sport holds that title. The [[@mango-tree|mango]] is often called the national fruit for similar reasons. When a list of national symbols seems very long, it is worth checking which ones a government actually adopted.

text: In a market, [[@money-shopping|prices]] are set by a tug-of-war between two things: supply, how much of something is available, and demand, how much people want it. When something is scarce and many people want it, its price rises. When there is plenty and few want it, its price falls.

No single person decides this. Thousands of sellers and buyers each make their own choices, and the price settles where the amount people want to buy roughly matches the amount on offer. The Scottish thinker Adam Smith described this in 1776, in a book called *The Wealth of Nations*.

st.prompt: Heavy rains damage tomato crops across several states, but people still want to buy just as many tomatoes. What happens to the price?
st.reveal: When supply falls but demand stays the same, buyers compete for fewer tomatoes, so sellers can charge more. When the next harvest arrives, supply rises and prices usually fall again.

myth: Shopkeepers simply charge whatever they like.

Sellers can set any price, but if it is too high, customers buy from someone else or not at all. Competition, costs and how much people want something keep pushing prices towards a level buyers will pay.
facts: The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith, 1776
Prices that change by the minute

sec.t:
For most of history, shoppers haggled. Buyer and seller argued back and forth until they agreed. In many Indian bazaars, that still happens. A seller starts high, the buyer offers less, and they meet somewhere in the middle.

In the 1800s, large department stores in cities like Paris, London and New York made fixed price tags common. They had too many customers and staff to haggle over every sale. Fixed prices made shopping faster, though the store still had to pick a price that people would pay.

An auction lets buyers compete openly. At big wholesale markets, called mandis in India, traders often bid for farmers' produce, and the highest bidder wins the load. [[@delhi|Delhi]]'s Azadpur Mandi is one of the largest fruit and vegetable markets in Asia.

Auctions can produce surprising prices. At the first auction of 2019 at Toyosu fish market in [[@tokyo|Tokyo]], a [[@sushi|sushi]] restaurant owner paid about 333 million yen for a single bluefin tuna. Part of that was for the fame of buying the year's first big fish.

Some prices now change by the minute. Airline tickets usually get pricier as seats fill up. Cab apps raise fares when many people want a ride at once, such as in heavy rain. The aim is to persuade more drivers to come out and some riders to wait. Shares of companies on stock markets change price every second during trading.

Prices also send signals. When a price rises, it tells farmers and factories to make more, and tells shoppers to buy less or switch to something else. When it falls, the opposite happens. Nobody plans this centrally, yet across a whole country it helps match what is made with what people want. Adam Smith called this the "invisible hand".

Markets are good at matching buyers and sellers, but not perfect. If a medicine or basic food becomes too expensive for poor families, governments may step in. India sets minimum support prices for some crops so farmers are not paid too little, and sells subsidised grain through ration shops. Economists argue about how much governments should interfere. Next to any [[@street-food|street food]] stall, you can watch the same forces at work: a vendor raising prices when the queue is long and offering deals when it is quiet.

text: A survey asks a small group of people some questions and uses their answers to estimate what a much larger group thinks or does. The small group is called a [[sample|sample]].

The trick is choosing the sample fairly, so that every kind of person has a fair chance of being picked. If you do, the laws of [[@probability|probability]] say the sample will usually look a lot like the whole population. A good poll of about 1,000 adults can estimate a national opinion to within about 3 [[percentage|percentage]] points, most of the time.

st.prompt: A survey asks 1,000 fairly chosen people a question. If you asked 4,000 instead, how much smaller would the margin of error get?

options.t: It would not change at all

st.reveal: The margin of error shrinks with the square root of the sample size. Four times the people gives only twice the accuracy, which is why pollsters rarely bother asking huge numbers.

d.try: Ask everyone in your class to pick their favourite of three snacks and count the answers. Then put the names in a bowl, draw out just ten, and see what those ten chose. Compare the small sample with the whole class. Try the draw a few times and see how much the result jumps around.
myth: A survey with more people in it is always more accurate.
Who you ask matters more than how many. A huge sample of the wrong people can be far worse than a small sample chosen fairly, as the 1936 Literary Digest poll showed.
facts: asking a sample of people instead of everyone

sec.t:
Pollsters like a kitchen comparison. To check whether a big pot of dal needs salt, you don't eat the whole pot. You stir it well and taste one spoonful. That spoonful works for a small pot or a giant wedding pot, as long as it was stirred.

Choosing people at random is the stirring. That is why a sample of 1,000 works almost as well for India as for a small country. What matters is how well you mixed the pot, not how big the pot is.

Even a perfect sample can be spoiled by a bad question. "Do you agree that our wonderful school needs a longer lunch break?" pushes people towards yes. Researchers call this a leading question.

Order matters too, and so does who asks. People may give the answer they think sounds good to a stranger, rather than the true one. Careful surveys test their questions first on small groups and keep the wording plain and neutral.

sec.h: Surveys in India and the USA
sec.t:
India runs some of the biggest surveys in the world. The National Family Health Survey visits hundreds of thousands of households and asks about health, children and [[nutrition|nutrition]]. Its results help governments decide where to send doctors and food programmes. The [[@census|census]] is different: it tries to count everyone, but only once every ten years.

In the USA, groups such as Gallup and the Pew Research Center publish regular polls on what Americans think. Around [[@polls-elections|elections]] in both countries, news channels report opinion polls and exit polls (questions asked to voters as they leave the polling booth). These are useful, but they have missed results before, so smart readers check the sample size and the [[@percentages|percentages]] carefully.

sec.h: Reading a poll like an expert
sec.t: When you see a poll in the news, look for three details: how many people were asked, how they were chosen, and the margin of error. If two candidates are 2 points apart and the margin of error is 3 points, the race is too close to call. That small line at the bottom of the chart often matters more than the big headline.

text: PV Sindhu is one of India's greatest badminton players. She won a silver medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics and a bronze at the 2020 Tokyo Games, held in 2021. That made her the first Indian woman to win two individual Olympic medals. In 2019 she became world champion, the first Indian to win the title.
She is tall, with a long reach and a powerful smash. On court she shouts loudly after winning points, and fans across India have learnt to roar with her.

st.reveal: Tournament shuttles use 16 feathers, usually from geese, fixed into a cork base. They make the shuttle shoot off the racket very fast and then slow down sharply, which is why a smash can be so hard to return.

Top players can smash the shuttle at more than 400 km/h, and a long rally can leave them as out of breath as a sprinter. Badminton has been an Olympic sport since 1992.

sec.t:
Sindhu was born in Hyderabad in 1995. Her parents, P. V. Ramana and P. Vijaya, both played volleyball at national level, and her father was part of the Indian team that won a bronze at the 1986 Asian Games.

Sindhu chose badminton after watching Pullela Gopichand win the All England Championship in 2001. Gopichand later opened an academy in Hyderabad, and Sindhu joined it. As a child she travelled about 56 kilometres a day between home and training, and practice often began before dawn.

At the Rio Olympics, Sindhu was ranked tenth in the world. She beat higher-ranked players one after another to reach the final, where she met Spain's Carolina Marín. Sindhu won the first game, but Marín came back to win.

Sindhu's silver was still a huge moment. She was 21, and millions of Indians had stayed up late to watch. Her rivalry with Marín became one of the best in women's badminton.

Before the Games, Gopichand had famously taken away her phone and cut out sweets so she could focus completely. After the Games she got both back, along with a lot of new followers. Back home in Hyderabad, crowds lined the roads for an open-bus parade, and several state governments gave her cash prizes and land.

{{story:reflexes}}

Sindhu won silver at the World Championships in 2017 and 2018. In 2017 she lost a final to Japan's Nozomi Okuhara after a 110-minute match, one of the longest women's singles finals ever.

In 2019, in Basel, [[@switzerland|Switzerland]], she met Okuhara again in the final. This time Sindhu won 21–7, 21–7 in under 40 minutes. She was the first Indian to become world champion in badminton. She dedicated the title to her mother, whose birthday it was.

At the Tokyo Games she lost the semi-final to Tai Tzu-ying of Taiwan, then beat China's He Bingjiao to win bronze. Her coach by then was Park Tae-sang of South Korea.

She has also won gold at the [[@commonwealth-games|Commonwealth Games]], in 2022 in Birmingham. [[@badminton-india|India's badminton]] is now strong across the board. Saina Nehwal won India's first Olympic badminton medal, a bronze in 2012. Players like Kidambi Srikanth and Lakshya Sen have won big titles too, and many trained in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]].

A shuttlecock has 16 feathers stuck into a cork base. When hit hard, it leaves the racket faster than a cricket ball off a bat, then slows sharply because the feathers catch the air. In 2023 India's Satwiksairaj Rankireddy set a Guinness World Record for the fastest badminton hit, at 565 km/h.

That means players must judge speed and angle in a split second. Sindhu trains her [[@reflexes|reflexes]], her legs and her footwork, and works on reading where the shuttle will go before it is hit.

लाल रक्त कोशिकाएँ तुम्हारे [[@lungs-breathe|फेफड़ों]] से ऑक्सीजन लेकर शरीर के कोने-कोने तक पहुँचाती हैं। सफ़ेद रक्त कोशिकाएँ कीटाणुओं से लड़ती हैं। [[platelet|प्लेटलेट्स]], यानी कोशिकाओं के नन्हे टुकड़े, चोट लगने पर रिसाव बंद करते हैं।

एक बड़े इंसान के शरीर में लगभग 5 लीटर खून होता है। यह मोटे तौर पर रसोई के तेल वाली एक बड़ी कैन जितना है। बच्चों में उनके कद के हिसाब से कम होता है। जब तुम आराम कर रहे होते हो, तब तुम्हारा [[@heart-beat|दिल]] लगभग एक मिनट में पूरे खून को शरीर का एक चक्कर लगवा देता है।

हर लाल कोशिका [[haemoglobin|हीमोग्लोबिन]] से ठसाठस भरी होती है। यह एक [[protein|प्रोटीन]] है जिसके बीच में लोहा होता है। हीमोग्लोबिन फेफड़ों में ऑक्सीजन पकड़ता है और मांसपेशियों और दिमाग में जाकर उसे छोड़ देता है। खून को लाल रंग भी यही देता है। पालक, दाल और मांस जैसे खाने में मौजूद लोहा शरीर को इसे बनाने में मदद करता है।

एक लाल कोशिका लगभग 120 दिन जीती है। फिर उसे तोड़कर उसका सामान दोबारा काम में ले लिया जाता है। कूल्हे और पसलियों जैसी [[@bones|हड्डियों]] के बीच का नरम गूदा, यानी बोन मैरो, हर सेकंड लगभग 20 लाख नई लाल कोशिकाएँ बनाता है।

प्लाज़्मा सिर्फ़ कोशिकाओं को नहीं ढोता। खाने से मिली शक्कर, नमक, विटामिन और [[@hormones|हॉर्मोन]], सब इसी में सवार होकर चलते हैं। कचरा भी, जैसे कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड, जो वापस फेफड़ों तक जाती है और साँस के साथ बाहर निकल जाती है। प्लाज़्मा गर्मी को भी पूरे शरीर में बाँटता है, जिससे पूरे शरीर का तापमान एक जैसा बना रहता है।

किसी ज़माने में लोग सोचते थे कि [[@liver|जिगर]] लगातार नया खून बनाता है और शरीर उसे खर्च कर देता है। 1628 में अंग्रेज़ डॉक्टर विलियम हार्वे ने दिखाया कि दिल एक ही खून को बार-बार गोल घेरे में पंप करता है। उन्होंने नापा कि हर धड़कन में दिल कितना खून बाहर धकेलता है। तब उन्हें समझ आया कि शरीर हर घंटे इतना सारा खून बना ही नहीं सकता। यानी वही खून घूम-फिरकर लौटता होगा।

इससे सदियों पहले अरब चिकित्सक इब्न अल-नफ़ीस बता चुके थे कि खून फेफड़ों से होकर गुज़रता है। हार्वे ने पूरे चक्कर को जोड़कर समझाया।

हर जानवर का खून लाल नहीं होता। [[@octopus-smart|ऑक्टोपस]] का खून नीला होता है, क्योंकि वह ऑक्सीजन ढोने के लिए लोहे की जगह ताँबे का इस्तेमाल करता है। हॉर्सशू केकड़ों का खून भी नीला होता है। इससे दवाओं और इंजेक्शनों की जाँच की जाती है कि कहीं उनमें खतरनाक बैक्टीरिया तो नहीं। न्यू गिनी की कुछ छिपकलियों का खून तो हरा होता है।

खून अभी किसी फ़ैक्ट्री में नहीं बनाया जा सकता, इसलिए अस्पताल खून देने वालों पर निर्भर रहते हैं। भारत में 18 से 65 साल के सेहतमंद लोग आम तौर पर [[@blood-donation|रक्तदान]] कर सकते हैं। अमेरिका के ज़्यादातर राज्यों में कम से कम उम्र 16 या 17 साल है। एक बार का दान कई ज़िंदगियाँ बचाने में मदद कर सकता है, क्योंकि खून को अक्सर लाल कोशिकाओं, प्लाज़्मा और प्लेटलेट्स में अलग करके अलग-अलग मरीज़ों को दिया जाता है। चढ़ाने से पहले उसका [[@blood-groups|ब्लड ग्रुप]] मिलाना ज़रूरी है।

text: जब भी तुम हिलते हो, दिमाग़ फटाफट अंदाज़ा लगाता है कि वह हरकत कैसी महसूस होगी। दिमाग़ के पिछले हिस्से में सेरिबेलम नाम का एक भाग इस अंदाज़े की तुलना उससे करता है जो तुम्हारी त्वचा असल में बताती है।

जब तुम खुद को गुदगुदी करने की कोशिश करते हो, तो अंदाज़ा लगभग सौ टका सही होता है। दिमाग़ ठीक-ठीक जानता है कि छुअन कब और कहाँ आएगी, इसलिए वह एहसास को धीमा कर देता है। जब कोई और गुदगुदी करता है, तो छुअन अचानक आती है। दिमाग़ उसे भाँप नहीं पाता, इसलिए एहसास पूरी ताकत से पहुँचता है। गुदगुदी को गुदगुदी बनाने में इसी अचानकपन का बड़ा हाथ है। इसी वजह से तुम्हें मुँह में अपनी जीभ का पता नहीं चलता, पर किसी और की उँगली का फ़ौरन चल जाता।

d.try: एक पंख या नरम पेंटब्रश अपनी हथेली पर धीरे-धीरे फिराओ, फिर किसी दोस्त से ठीक यही करने को कहो। दोनों बार 0 से 10 तक नंबर दो कि कितनी गुदगुदी हुई। फिर जब दोस्त ब्रश फिरा रहा हो, तब अपना हाथ हल्के से उसके हाथ के ऊपर रख दो, और फिर नंबर दो।
myth: अगर कोई गुदगुदी पर हँस रहा है, तो उसे ज़रूर मज़ा आ रहा है।
गुदगुदी पर हँसी कुछ हद तक अपने आप आती है। बहुत-से लोग इसे सच में नापसंद करते हुए भी ज़ोर से हँसते हैं, इसलिए हँसी का मतलब यह नहीं कि वे और चाहते हैं। "बस करो" कहना हमेशा ठीक है।
facts: अपनी हरकतों को पहले से भाँपने वाला दिमाग़ का हिस्सा

sec.t:
वैज्ञानिक दो तरह की गुदगुदी बताते हैं। पहली हल्की, रेंगती-सी होती है, जैसे बाँह पर चलती चींटी या गाल पर पंख। इससे खुजलाने या झाड़ने का मन करता है। यह शायद जानवरों को अपनी त्वचा पर कीड़ों और [[parasite|परजीवियों]] का पता लगाने में मदद करती है।

दूसरी गहरी, कोंचने वाली गुदगुदी है, पसलियों, बगलों या तलवों पर, जिससे लोग हँसते और छटपटाते हैं। इसके लिए ज़्यादातर किसी दूसरे इंसान की ज़रूरत होती है। ये जगहें वे भी हैं जहाँ शरीर नरम है और आसानी से चोट लग सकती है। इसी वजह से कुछ वैज्ञानिक सोचते हैं कि गुदगुदी शायद खेल-खेल में बच्चों को इन जगहों को बचाना सिखाती है।

गुदगुदी पर सिर्फ़ इंसान ही नहीं हँसते। दूसरे [[mammal|स्तनधारी]] भी हँसते हैं। छोटे चिंपैंज़ी और गोरिल्ला गुदगुदी वाले खेलों में हाँफती-सी हँसी हँसते हैं। 1990 के दशक में अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक याक पैंकसेप ने पाया कि पेट पर गुदगुदी करने पर चूहे बहुत ऊँची चीं-चीं करते हैं। यह आवाज़ इतनी ऊँची है कि हम सुन नहीं पाते, पर चमगादड़ों की आवाज़ पकड़ने वाला यंत्र इसे पकड़ लेता है।

गुदगुदी वाले चूहे फिर से गुदगुदी करवाने के लिए वैज्ञानिक के हाथ के पीछे भागते थे, जिससे लगता है कि उन्हें यह अच्छा लगता था। उनकी चीं-चीं [[ultrasound|अल्ट्रासाउंड]] है, यानी ऐसी ध्वनि तरंगें जो इंसानी कानों के लिए बहुत तेज़ी से काँपती हैं, जैसे [[@bats-fly|चमगादड़ों]] की पुकार।

गुदगुदी अजीब चीज़ है, क्योंकि यह एक साथ मज़ेदार भी हो सकती है और बुरी भी। बहुत-से लोग गुदगुदी पसंद न होने पर भी ज़ोर से हँसते हैं, क्योंकि हँसी कुछ हद तक अपने आप आती है, कुछ-कुछ [[@reflexes|प्रतिवर्त क्रिया]] की तरह। इसलिए गुदगुदी में हँसी का मतलब हमेशा "और करो" नहीं होता।

गुदगुदी आमतौर पर एक-दूसरे को अच्छी तरह जानने वाले लोगों का खेल है, जैसे माता-पिता और शिशु, या भाई-बहन। शिशु लगभग चार महीने की उम्र में गुदगुदी पर हँसना शुरू करते हैं। मूड भी मायने रखता है। जब तुम घबराए हुए या नाराज़ हो, तो गुदगुदी में कहीं कम मज़ा आता है। इससे पता चलता है कि इस सीधे-सादे एहसास को भी [[@brain-works|दिमाग़]] कितना गढ़ता है। ज़्यादातर लोग अपनी [[@skin|त्वचा]] पर हल्की खुजली तो महसूस करा सकते हैं, पर अपनी ही उँगलियों से खुद को हँसा पाना लगभग किसी के बस का नहीं।

text: Your heart has its own built-in electrical timer, a small patch of cells that fires a pulse about once a second. If that timer slows down or the signal gets blocked, the heart can beat too slowly. A person may feel faint, tired or dizzy.

A pacemaker takes over the job. It is a small metal case with a battery and a [[circuit|circuit]], placed under the skin near the collarbone. Thin wires run to the heart and deliver a tiny pulse whenever the heart needs one.

One of its inventors found the key idea by accident. In 1956, an American engineer named Wilson Greatbatch put the wrong part into a circuit, and it began to pulse in the [[rhythm|rhythm]] of a heartbeat.

st.prompt: Greatbatch needed a resistor of 10,000 ohms. He grabbed one that was 100 times too big. What did his circuit do?

options.t: It sent out a short pulse, paused about a second, then pulsed again

st.reveal: The wrong resistor made the circuit squirt out a tiny electrical pulse, rest, and repeat. Greatbatch recognised the rhythm at once. It was just like a heartbeat.

sec.t:
Greatbatch was not the only one working on the idea. In the early 1950s, American doctors used pacemakers as big as a microwave oven, plugged into the wall. Patients had to stay close to a socket. In 1957, after a power cut put patients at risk, Earl Bakken in Minnesota built a battery pacemaker small enough to wear.

The first one placed fully inside a person's body came in 1958, in Stockholm. The engineer Rune Elmqvist and the [[surgeon|surgeon]] Åke Senning built it for Arne Larsson, a 43-year-old whose heart kept stopping. His wife had pleaded with them to try. The first device failed within hours, and the backup also lasted only a short time. But the idea worked.

Greatbatch and the surgeon William Chardack implanted their own design in a patient in Buffalo in 1960. It was soon made and sold widely.

Early pacemakers ran on [[@batteries-history|batteries]] that lasted only a year or two. Every time they died, patients needed another operation. Some batteries also leaked inside the body.

Greatbatch spent years on this problem too. In the 1970s he helped develop a lithium-iodide battery for pacemakers that could last ten years or more. Most implanted pacemakers in the following decades used this type.

The first wearable pacemakers were about the size of a paperback book. Most today are close to the size of a matchbox and weigh around 20 to 30 g, about as much as an AA battery.

Some newer models skip wires altogether. These leadless pacemakers are about the size of a large [[vitamin|vitamin]] pill and sit right inside the heart, fed in through a [[vein|vein]] in the leg. They also sense when you are running or climbing stairs, and speed up the beat to match, much as your own [[@heart-beat|heart]] would.

sec.h: A spark that runs the body
sec.t:
Larsson lived with pacemakers for 43 years. He died in 2001, aged 86, after outliving both Elmqvist and Senning. Today more than a million pacemakers are fitted around the world every year.

The pacemaker works because the heart is, in a sense, electrical. So is the rest of you, and the same kind of tiny pulses that it copies are firing right now along the wires of your [[@nervous-system|nervous system]].

text: A typeface is a design for a set of letters, numbers and symbols. Times New Roman, Arial and Comic Sans are typefaces. Strictly speaking, a font is one version of a typeface: a single size and style, such as 12-point bold. Today most people use the two words to mean the same thing.

Fonts change how words feel. The same sentence can look serious, friendly, old-fashioned or futuristic depending on the letters. Designers choose fonts for books, road signs, apps and food packets to make them easy to read and to give them the right mood. Every one of those letter shapes was drawn by someone.

myth: Special fonts can cure dyslexia.

Some fonts are designed to be easier for people with dyslexia, and some readers like them. But careful studies have not found that these fonts make people read much faster or better. Larger text, more space between letters and lines, and good teaching seem to help more.

sec.t:
Before computers, fonts were real objects. After Johannes Gutenberg developed his [[@printing-press|printing press]] in Germany around 1450, every letter was cast as a small block of metal. A complete set of one size and style was called a font, or fount in older British spelling, from a French word for something cast in metal.

Typesetters picked letters out of wooden trays called cases and lined them up by hand, backwards, to make each line. Capitals sat in the upper case and small letters in the lower case. That's where the names come from. Setting one page could take hours.

Many typefaces have serifs: small feet or flicks at the ends of the strokes. Look at a capital T in a newspaper and you may see tiny lines at the tips. Serifs go back to letters carved in stone in [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]]. Experts still argue about whether the carvers added them for beauty or because of the way their brushes and chisels worked.

Typefaces without these feet are called sans serif, from the French word for "without". They look cleaner and more modern. Many apps and road signs use sans serif fonts because they stay clear at small sizes and from far away.

Printing in Indian scripts took longer, because letters join and change shape in many ways. In 1778, Charles Wilkins, an Englishman in Bengal, worked with a local craftsman named Panchanan Karmakar to cut the first Bengali printing type. Karmakar went on to cut type for other Indian scripts too.

Digital fonts for [[@scripts-india|Indian scripts]] are still tricky. A Devanagari or Tamil font needs hundreds of shapes for joined letters and vowel signs. [[@unicode|Unicode]] gives each letter a number, but the font must know how to draw each combination. When it can't, you see empty boxes, nicknamed "tofu". Google named its huge free font family Noto, from "no more tofu", with the aim of covering every script in use.

Good designers match the font to the job. A storybook for young children might use round, simple letters. A legal form might use a plain serif font. A horror film poster might use spiky, dripping letters. Text in apps must stay clear on small, bright screens.

Fonts are also linked to the history of writing tools. Styles from [[@typewriters-keyboards|typewriters]], where every letter took up the same width, still appear in coding programs today. Someone sat down and drew every letter you are reading right now, including this full stop.

text: In the 1700s, thirteen British colonies stretched along the east coast of North America. The people living there were ruled from London, more than 5,000 km away across the Atlantic.

After an expensive war, Britain began taxing the colonists to pay its bills. The colonists had no members in Britain's Parliament, so they had no say in those taxes. "No taxation without representation" became their cry. Protests turned into fighting in 1775. In 1776 the colonies declared themselves independent, and after eight years of war they won. The new country was the United States of America.

st.reveal: Men boarded three ships and threw 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor. In today's money the tea would have been worth well over a million dollars. Britain responded by closing the harbour.

Congress approved the wording on 4 July. Most delegates signed the handwritten copy on 2 August 1776, and a few signed even later.

sec.t:
From 1754 to 1763, Britain fought France for control of North America in what the colonists called the French and Indian War. Britain won, but the war cost a fortune, and keeping soldiers in America cost more.

London decided the colonies should help pay. The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed newspapers, [[@cards-games|playing cards]] and legal papers. Later laws taxed glass, paint, paper and tea. Each new tax led to boycotts and protests, and some were dropped. In 1770, British soldiers in [[@boston|Boston]] fired into a crowd that was taunting them and throwing snowballs, killing five people. Colonists called it the Boston Massacre. The anger stayed.

Britain punished Boston by closing its harbour. In April 1775, British soldiers marched out to seize weapons stored at Concord, near Boston. [[colonial|Colonial]] fighters met them at Lexington and Concord, and the war began.

The colonies' Congress chose [[@george-washington|George Washington]] of Virginia to lead their army. His soldiers were often short of food, boots and pay. Some were teenagers, and some were Black soldiers, free and enslaved, who fought on both sides. During the winter of 1777–78 at Valley Forge, thousands fell ill in the cold camp.

On 4 July 1776, Congress approved the [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|Declaration of Independence]], written mostly by [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]]. Its most famous line says that "all men are created equal" and have rights to "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness".

Those words did not apply to everyone yet. About one in five people in the colonies was enslaved, and women and Native Americans were left out. Later generations used the same words to demand their own rights.

The turning point came in 1777, when Americans defeated a British army at Saratoga in New York. France then joined the war on America's side, bringing ships, soldiers and money.

In October 1781, French and American forces trapped General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, and he surrendered. The Treaty of Paris in 1783 recognised the United States as independent. A few years later the new nation wrote its [[@us-constitution|Constitution]].

Cornwallis, meanwhile, became Governor-General of India in 1786. Britain had lost thirteen colonies in America, but it was steadily gaining power in India. Every 4 July, Americans celebrate with parades and [[@fireworks|fireworks]].

text: Sarojini Naidu was a poet and one of the best-known leaders of India's freedom struggle. Her poems, written in English, were so musical that people called her the Nightingale of India.

She later put much of her writing aside to work with [[@gandhi|Gandhi]]. She gave fiery speeches across India and abroad, marched in the [[@salt-march|Salt Satyagraha]], and went to prison. She became the first Indian woman to lead the Indian National Congress, and after independence the first woman to govern an Indian state.

She never held either job. She was the first woman to be governor of an Indian state, the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh), from 1947 until her death in 1949.

sec.t:
Sarojini Chattopadhyay was born in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]] in 1879, the eldest of eight children. Her father, Aghorenath, was a scientist who helped found the city's Nizam College. Her mother wrote poetry in Bengali.

Sarojini was quick. She passed her matriculation exam at 12 and wrote a long poem at 13. The Nizam of Hyderabad gave her a scholarship to study in England, at King's College London and then Girton College, Cambridge.

In England, the critic Edmund Gosse read her early poems, which copied English styles about robins and snow. He told her to write about India instead: its temples, markets and people.

She took the advice. Her first book, *The Golden Threshold*, came out in London in 1905 and was named after her family home. Her poems described bangle sellers, palanquin bearers and the spice and silver of Hyderabad's bazaars. They were full of [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] and colour, meant to be read aloud.

{{story:poetry}}

At 19 she married Dr Govindarajulu Naidu, a doctor from another region and community. Marriages across communities were rare at the time and drew disapproval. The couple went ahead anyway and had four children.

Meetings with leaders such as Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Gandhi drew her into politics. She travelled across India speaking about freedom and about women's education and rights. In 1925 she was elected president of the Congress.

In 1930, Gandhi began his march to the sea to make salt in defiance of British law. After he was arrested, Naidu led a protest at the Dharasana salt works in Gujarat. Hundreds of volunteers walked forward, unarmed, towards police lines. Reports of their courage spread around the world.

She was jailed several times. She also went with Gandhi to London in 1931 for the Round Table Conference, where Indian leaders and the British government discussed India's future. The talks failed, but her speeches won many friends for India's cause.

Naidu was famous for her humour. She was one of the few people who teased Gandhi openly, and she nicknamed him "Mickey Mouse" because of his big ears. Gandhi enjoyed the joke and wrote her warm, playful letters in return.

She also spoke up for women's right to vote and take part in public life. She was part of a delegation in 1917 asking the British for votes for Indian women, part of a [[@womens-vote|worldwide fight for the vote]].

When India became free in 1947, she was made governor of the United Provinces, now Uttar Pradesh. She died in office in Lucknow on 2 March 1949.

Her birthday, 13 February, is marked as National Women's Day in India. Her old home in Hyderabad, The Golden Threshold, now belongs to the University of Hyderabad, and students study there.

text: The Everglades are a vast [[wetland|wetland]] in southern Florida, in the United States. Water spills out of a big lake, Lake Okeechobee, and spreads south in a shallow sheet, often less than knee-deep, flowing slowly to the sea. Tall sawgrass grows out of the water as far as you can see, dotted with islands of trees.

The area is home to alligators, crocodiles, wading birds, manatees and the rare Florida panther. It also supplies drinking water to millions of people in cities such as [[@miami|Miami]]. About half of the original Everglades has been drained for farms and cities. Since 2000, the USA has been running a long and costly plan to restore what is left.

st.reveal: Burmese pythons, probably released or escaped pets, have spread through the Everglades since the 1980s and 1990s. With no natural enemies there, they eat many small mammals and birds. Florida pays hunters and runs contests to remove them.

Slowly pour water at the high end and watch how it spreads and seeps rather than rushing. That gentle sheet of water is how the Everglades moves.
myth: The Everglades is just a big, stagnant swamp.
The water is always moving, though very slowly. It flows south as a wide, shallow sheet from Lake Okeechobee towards Florida Bay. That is why Marjory Stoneman Douglas called it a "river of grass".
