sec.t:
The Everglades are so flat that the land drops only a few centimetres for every kilometre. Water creeps across this slope so slowly that a single drop can take months to travel from the lake to the coast. In many places, the "river" is about 100 kilometres wide.

In 1947, the writer Marjory Stoneman Douglas published a book called *The Everglades: River of Grass*. Many people had thought of the area as a useless swamp to be drained. Her book showed them a living river and helped turn public opinion. In the same year, Everglades National Park was opened to protect the southern part.

Where the river of grass meets the sea, it turns into a maze of [[@mangroves|mangroves]], trees that can grow in salty water on stilt-like roots. These forests shelter baby fish, protect the coast from storm waves and soak up mud. Visitors to India's [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]] would find the scenery familiar, though Florida swaps the tigers for alligators and panthers.

The Seminole and Miccosukee peoples have lived in and around the Everglades for about 200 years, and other Native American groups lived there for thousands of years before them. They know its channels and islands better than anyone.

In the late 1800s and 1900s, people began digging canals to drain the Everglades. They wanted dry land for sugarcane fields, vegetable farms and growing cities. Dykes and pumps sent water straight to the sea, and the slow, wide sheet of water was cut into pieces.

The results were serious. Bird numbers fell sharply. Some areas dried out and burned in wildfires. Salt water seeped into wells along the coast. Today, the original Everglades is about half its former size.

sec.h: New threats and a big repair
sec.t:
Animals from other places now cause trouble too. Burmese pythons, large snakes from Southeast Asia that were probably pets, have spread through the park. With no natural enemies, they eat rabbits, raccoons and birds. They are one of the best-known examples of an [[@invasive-species|invasive species]] anywhere.

In 2000, the US government approved a huge restoration plan to send more clean water south again, the way it used to flow. Work on it will take decades. The park has been a World Heritage Site since 1979, and for many years it has also been on UNESCO's list of sites in danger.

text: The Gateway of India is a huge stone arch on the waterfront in south [[@mumbai|Mumbai]]. It faces the harbour, at a spot once called Apollo Bunder. It is about 26 m tall, about as high as an eight-storey building.
It was built to remember the visit of the British king George V and Queen Mary in December 1911. Work began in 1913 and finished in 1924.
Today it is one of Mumbai's best-known sights. Crowds gather around it at all hours, pigeons fill the square, and ferries leave from the steps nearby for Elephanta Island and Mandwa.

st.reveal: On 28 February 1948, the last British troops in India marched through the Gateway and boarded a ship home. The arch built to celebrate British arrival ended up marking the British departure.

myth: King George V and Queen Mary landed through the Gateway of India.
The Gateway was only an idea when they arrived in 1911. Its foundation stone was laid in 1913 and it opened in 1924, long after they had gone home.

sec.t:
In 1911 King George V became the first reigning British monarch to visit India. He and Queen Mary arrived by sea at Bombay, as the city was then called. A grand welcome had to be laid on fast. So the royal couple stepped ashore under a temporary arch made largely of cardboard and plaster.

The city decided to build a permanent gateway on the spot. A Scottish architect, George Wittet, drew the design. The foundation stone was laid in March 1913.

First the ground had to be made. The sea along the shore was filled in and a new sea wall built. The arch itself took years more. It cost about 21 lakh rupees, a vast sum at the time. It was finally opened in December 1924, thirteen years after the visit it was meant to remember.

The Gateway is built of yellow [[basalt|basalt]], a [[@rocks-types|volcanic rock]] common around Mumbai, with reinforced concrete inside. Its style is called Indo-Saracenic, a mix that British architects in India loved.

Look closely and you can find pointed arches from Islamic buildings, carved stone screens called jalis and decorations borrowed from Hindu and Jain temples. Many people say the arch looks a bit like Gujarati buildings from the 1500s. The central arch is wide and tall, with four towers on top.

Wittet also helped design other Mumbai buildings in the same style, including the Prince of Wales Museum, now called the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya.

The Gateway was built to show British power. It ended up marking the end of it.

India became independent in August 1947. Over the next months, British troops sailed home. On 28 February 1948, the last soldiers, the First Battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry, marched through the Gateway in a ceremony and boarded a ship. Indian troops gave them a farewell salute.

So the arch built to welcome a British king became the door through which the last British soldiers left. Many people see it as a symbol of India's [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]] reaching its end.

{{story:sea-ports}}

Opposite the Gateway stands the Taj Mahal Palace hotel, which opened in 1903, even before the arch. The two buildings together are one of the most photographed views in India. Security around both was tightened after the 2008 attacks on Mumbai, when the hotel was one of the places targeted.

The Gateway is lit up for festivals and national days, and its square fills with crowds on Diwali, New Year and Independence Day. Boats bob in the harbour, and hawkers sell roasted peanuts and balloons. Mumbai's sea breeze carries salt, which slowly eats at the stone, so the arch is cleaned and repaired from time to time. Its basalt has also darkened in places from traffic smoke and sea spray.

In the evening, the arch glows golden in its lights against the dark water. Many visitors from other parts of India and abroad begin their trip to Mumbai right here, as it was always meant to be, a gateway.

text: The Modhera Sun Temple in Gujarat was built about a thousand years ago for Surya, the Hindu Sun god. Its builders lined it up so that on the [[equinox|equinoxes]], in March and September, the rising sun shines straight through the doorway and into the inner shrine, where Surya's image once stood.

Today no regular worship happens there. Instead, visitors come to see its carvings, its huge stepped tank and, each January, a dance festival. At night, a light show plays across the stone. And the village around it now runs on sunlight in a very modern way.

st.reveal: The Surya Kund is lined with many small shrines, often counted as 108, a sacred number in Hindu tradition. They sit on the steps among the zigzag stairways down to the water.

sec.t:
The temple stands on the bank of the small Pushpavati river in Mehsana district. It was built under Bhima I, a king of the Chaulukya [[dynasty|dynasty]], also called the Solankis. An [[inscription|inscription]] on a wall gives a date of 1026–27 CE.

That is just after the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud of Ghazni raided Gujarat in 1024–25. Some historians think the temple may honour the people who fought him. Others think it was simply a royal gift to the Sun.

The temple has three parts lined up east to west. First comes the Surya Kund, the stepped tank. Then a dance hall with carved pillars. Then the shrine hall, where the god lived. On the summer [[solstice|solstice]], the noon Sun stands almost straight overhead here, because Modhera lies very close to the Tropic of Cancer.

sec.h: A tank like an upside-down pyramid

sec.t:
Almost every surface is carved. Pillars show dancers, musicians, animals and scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. On the shrine walls, 12 forms of Surya appear, one for each month of the year. Many wear tall boots, a sign of styles that came from Central Asia and Persia.

Parts of the temple were damaged in later wars, and the main image of Surya has long been lost. Even so, the carvings that survive are so crisp that you can count the beads on a dancer's necklace.

Every January, just after the kite festival of Uttarayan, Gujarat Tourism holds the Modhera Dance Festival on the temple's steps. Dancers perform classical styles like Bharatanatyam, Kathak and Odissi with the lit-up temple behind them. It has been held since 1992.

Since 2022, a 3D projection show lights up the temple at night, telling its history in colour on the old stone.

In October 2022, Modhera village was declared India's first village powered by the Sun around the clock. More than a thousand homes got [[@solar-india|solar panels]] on their roofs, and a solar farm with large batteries keeps power flowing after dark.

Some families now sell spare electricity back to the grid. A thousand years ago, people here prayed to the Sun. Now they also pay their bills with it. Another great Sun temple stands at [[@konark|Konark]] in Odisha. It is carved as a stone chariot, and some of its 24 giant wheels work as sundials.

text: Carlsbad Caverns is a national park in the Guadalupe Mountains of New Mexico, in the southwestern USA. Beneath its dry, cactus-covered hills lie about 120 known caves. The most famous is Carlsbad Cavern itself, which holds the Big Room, about 3.3 hectares in size. It is the largest cave chamber in North America that visitors can easily reach.

Inside are stone icicles, giant columns and delicate formations like soda straws. Every summer evening, hundreds of thousands of bats fly out of the entrance to hunt. The caves were carved in an unusual way, by [[acid|acid]], inside the remains of a reef that grew in a sea about 265 million years ago.

st.prompt: The rock around Carlsbad Caverns is limestone. What was that limestone, millions of years ago?

options.t: A reef in an ancient sea

st.reveal: About 265 million years ago, a shallow inland sea covered the area. Sponges, algae and other sea life built a long reef. Today that reef, called the Capitan Reef, forms the Guadalupe Mountains, and the caves are hollowed out inside it.

d.try: Grow your own stalactite. Dissolve lots of Epsom salt or washing soda in two jars of warm water. Set the jars apart with a plate between them, and drape a woolly string from one jar to the other with its middle sagging over the plate. Over a week, crystals drip and grow from the string.
myth: Stalactites and stalagmites are made of ice.
They are made of stone, mostly a mineral called calcite. Each drip of water leaves a thin film of mineral behind, and over thousands of years the films build up into stone icicles and columns.

sec.t:
Hard to believe, but this desert was once underwater. About 265 million years ago, a shallow inland sea covered the region. Along its edge, sponges, [[algae|algae]] and shellfish built a reef hundreds of kilometres long, much as corals build reefs today.

The sea dried up and the reef was buried. Much later, the land was pushed upwards, and the old reef became the Guadalupe Mountains. [[fossil|Fossils]] of ancient sea creatures can still be spotted in the cave walls, as the story of [[@fossils-form|how fossils form]] explains.

Most limestone caves are made by rainwater, which is slightly acidic and slowly eats away rock. Carlsbad is different. Deep below, there are large deposits of oil and gas. Gas called hydrogen sulphide, which smells like rotten eggs, seeped upwards from them.

When that gas met oxygen-rich groundwater, it formed sulphuric acid, a strong acid. The acid [[dissolve|dissolved]] huge spaces in the limestone, mostly between about 4 and 6 million years ago. The [[@oil-coal|oil]] far underground, in other words, helped hollow out the caves.

About 400,000 Brazilian free-tailed bats spend summers in one part of the cavern. At sunset, they spiral out of the entrance and head off to hunt moths and other insects. They use [[@echolocation|echolocation]], clicking and listening for echoes, to catch prey in the dark.

The park has seats near the entrance for watching the bat flight. Phones and cameras are not allowed during it, because noise and light can confuse the bats.

Local people had long known the cave was there, and Native Americans left pictures near its entrance. Around 1898, a teenager named Jim White saw what looked like smoke rising from the ground. It was bats. He explored the cave with a homemade wire ladder and a kerosene lamp.

White later guided visitors and told everyone about its wonders. Miners dug out bat droppings, called guano, to sell as [[fertiliser|fertiliser]]. In 1923 the cave became a national monument, and in 1930 a national park.

In 1986, cavers digging in a nearby pit broke through into Lechuguilla Cave. It has since been mapped for more than 225 km and goes 489 m deep. Inside are gypsum crystals several metres long and pools of perfectly clear water. [[microbe|Microbes]] living in it, cut off for millions of years, turned out to resist many [[antibiotic|antibiotics]]. Lechuguilla is closed to tourists to protect it. How such underground worlds begin is told in [[@caves-form|how caves form]].

text: Amar Chitra Katha is a series of Indian comic books started in 1967 by Anant Pai in Bombay. The name means "immortal picture stories". Each comic tells one story, from the Ramayana and the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] to the lives of emperors, freedom fighters and scientists, in about 30 colourful pages.

The comics brought history and [[mythology|mythology]] to children who might never read a thick history book. For decades, they were sold at railway stations, lent between friends and read on long train journeys. Many Indian adults say they first met [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], Shivaji or the Rani of Jhansi in its pages.

sec.h: A quiz that started it all
sec.t:
Anant Pai had worked on comics for a Bombay newspaper group. In 1967, as he often told the story, he watched a TV quiz from Delhi. The children could answer questions about [[@greek-myths|Greek gods]] but not about Rama's mother. Pai felt Indian children were losing touch with their own stories.

He persuaded the publishers India Book House to try comics. The first titles were Indian versions of Western [[@fairy-tales|fairy tales]] like Jack and the Beanstalk. They didn't do well. The series took off once it turned to Indian stories, starting with Krishna.

Over the years, the series published hundreds of titles. Some retold the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the Mahabharata in many parts. Others told history: [[@shivaji|Shivaji]], the [[@rani-lakshmibai|Rani of Jhansi]], Ashoka, Akbar and [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]]. There were saints and teachers of many faiths, including Guru Nanak, Kabir, the Buddha and Mahavira.

Folk stories had their place too, with [[@akbar-birbal|Akbar and Birbal]], [[@tenali-raman|Tenali Raman]] and [[@jataka-tales|Jataka tales]]. Later comics covered scientists, sports heroes and modern leaders.

In 1980, Pai started [[@tinkle|Tinkle]], a children's magazine. Its funny characters, like the foolish Suppandi and the hunter Shikari Shambu, became household names.

Amar Chitra Katha is often praised for getting millions of children interested in their country's past. It was published in English and in many Indian languages, and has sold tens of millions of copies.

Scholars have also raised fair criticisms. Some say the early comics tended to show heroes as fair-skinned and villains as dark. Others felt certain communities or rulers were shown one-sidedly, and that myth and history were sometimes mixed together. Readers today often enjoy the comics while also learning history from other sources.

Anant Pai died in 2011, but the comics continue, now also as digital editions and apps. The look of the old comics, with their bright colours and bold outlines, is part of the wider story of [[@comics-india|comics in India]].

Superhero comics from America, which took off in the 1930s and 1940s, mostly invented new heroes. Amar Chitra Katha did something different. It turned stories that were already thousands of years old into comics, and showed that real history could be as exciting as any invented [[@superheroes-history|superhero]].

text: Indian stories are packed with creatures that never walked the Earth. There are serpent people called nagas, the eagle-like [[@myths-garuda|Garuda]], a seven-headed flying horse, a two-headed bird strong enough to carry elephants, and water monsters with elephant trunks.

They come from old epics like the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and Mahabharata, from the Puranas, from Buddhist and Jain tales, and from village folk stories. Many still look down from temple walls, sit on state emblems and appear in comics. Some are guardians and some are vehicles for gods and goddesses. Others are [[trickster|tricksters]], ghosts or nature spirits. The same creature can look quite different in Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Bengal, because each region told the stories its own way.

Many are mixed or even heroic. In the Ramayana, the rakshasa Vibhishana sides with Rama. In the Mahabharata, Ghatotkacha, son of the Pandava Bhima and the rakshasi Hidimbi, fights bravely for his family.

sec.t:
Walk into an old South Indian temple and look at the pillars. You may see a yali, a creature with a lion's body and sometimes an elephant's trunk, rearing up on its back legs. Yalis were carved as protectors, and some are taller than a person.

Over doorways, you'll often find a makara: part crocodile, part fish, with a curling elephant trunk or tail. The river goddess Ganga rides one. Makaras gape over gateways from Sanchi to Cambodia and appear on jewellery too. Sculptors loved them because a makara could twist into any shape a doorway needed, one of the tricks of [[@temple-sculpture|temple sculpture]].

Gandaberunda is a giant bird with two heads facing opposite ways. In stories it is so strong it can carry an elephant in each claw. The kings of Vijayanagara and later the Wodeyar rulers of Mysore used it as a royal symbol. Today it sits on Karnataka's state emblem and appears in carvings at the [[@mysore-palace|Mysore Palace]].

Odisha has its own wonder: the Navagunjara, made of nine animals. It has a rooster's head, a peacock's neck, a lion's waist, a snake's tail and more. In the Odia poet Sarala Das's Mahabharata, Arjuna meets it and realises it is Krishna in disguise. Pattachitra painters in Puri still paint it.

Not every creature is grand. Folk tales are full of bhoots (ghosts) whose feet point backwards, and of the chudail, a frightening spirit in North Indian stories. The vetala is a spirit who lives in corpses at cremation grounds. In [[@vikram-betal|Vikram and Betal]], a clever vetala hangs from a tree and asks King Vikram a riddle every time he's carried off.

Yakshas are nature spirits who guard wealth and forests. In one famous Mahabharata story, a yaksha guarding a lake asks Yudhishthira a long string of questions before letting the brothers drink. Kinnaras, part human and part bird or horse, are heavenly musicians. Many cultures dreamed up similar mixtures, which is why scholars compare Indian creatures with Greek griffins and the [[@myths-unicorns|unicorns]] of [[medieval|medieval]] Europe.

text: कॉफ़ी एक झाड़ी से आती है, जिसका जंगली घर पूर्वी अफ़्रीका में [[@ethiopia|इथियोपिया]] के पहाड़ी जंगल हैं। इसके लाल फलों को चेरी कहते हैं, और हर फल में दो बीज होते हैं। यही बीज सुखाकर, भूनकर और पीसकर कॉफ़ी बनते हैं।

sec.t:
एक मशहूर कहानी इथियोपिया के काल्दी नाम के एक चरवाहे की है। उसने देखा कि एक ख़ास झाड़ी के [[@berries|लाल फल]] खाने के बाद उसकी बकरियाँ उछल-कूद मचाने लगती हैं। उसने ख़ुद भी चखे और उसमें ग़ज़ब की फुर्ती आ गई।

कहानी प्यारी है, पर इसका पहला लिखा रूप 1671 में आया, यानी कॉफ़ी के मशहूर होने के सदियों बाद। इतिहासकार इसे किंवदंती मानते हैं। [[botanist|वनस्पति वैज्ञानिक]] जो पक्का जानते हैं, वह यह है कि दुनिया में सबसे ज़्यादा पी जाने वाली अरेबिका कॉफ़ी इथियोपिया से आई है, और वहाँ के जंगलों में आज भी जंगली कॉफ़ी उगती है।

यमन का बंदरगाह मोका पूरे अरब जगत में कॉफ़ी भेजता था, इसीलिए "मोका" आज भी कॉफ़ी से जुड़ा शब्द है। 1550 के दशक तक इस्तांबुल में कॉफ़ी हाउस खुल गए थे, जहाँ लोग गपशप करने, खेल खेलने और ख़बरों पर बहस करने जुटते थे।

1600 के दशक में कॉफ़ी हाउस [[@venice|वेनिस]], लंदन और पेरिस तक फैल गए। लंदन में कुछ कॉफ़ी हाउस ख़ास धंधों से इतने जुड़ गए कि आगे चलकर मशहूर कंपनियाँ बन गए। कॉफ़ी उन्हीं समुद्री [[@trade-routes|व्यापार मार्गों]] से सफ़र करती थी, जिनसे मसाले और कपड़ा जाते थे।

बहुत समय तक यमन अपनी कॉफ़ी की कड़ी रखवाली करता रहा। वह बस भुने या उबले बीज बेचता था, जिनसे पौधा नहीं उग सकता था। एक मशहूर किंवदंती के मुताबिक़ 1600 के दशक में बाबा बुदन नाम के एक सूफ़ी संत हज की [[pilgrimage|तीर्थयात्रा]] से लौटते हुए सात बीज छिपाकर ले आए और उन्हें कर्नाटक के चिकमगलूर की पहाड़ियों में बो दिया। उन पहाड़ियों को आज बाबा बुदनगिरि कहते हैं।

आज भारत की लगभग 70% कॉफ़ी कर्नाटक में उगती है, और बाक़ी का बड़ा हिस्सा [[@kerala|केरल]] और तमिलनाडु में। इसका ज़्यादातर हिस्सा ऊँचे पेड़ों की छाँव में, काली मिर्च की बेलों और इलायची के साथ उगता है। वहाँ से कुछ ही दूर [[@bengaluru|बेंगलुरु]] के कैफ़े शहर के प्रोग्रामरों की नींद भगाए रखते हैं।

sec.h: फ़िल्टर कॉफ़ी और स्टील का गिलास
sec.t:
दक्षिण भारत में कॉफ़ी दो हिस्सों वाले धातु के फ़िल्टर में बनती है। ऊपर के हिस्से में पिसी कॉफ़ी रखी जाती है, गर्म पानी उसमें से धीरे-धीरे टपकता है, और नीचे एक गाढ़ा, गहरा अर्क जमा होता है, जिसे डिकॉक्शन कहते हैं। इसमें उबला दूध और चीनी मिलाई जाती है।

यह कॉफ़ी स्टील के गिलास में परोसी जाती है, जो एक चौड़ी कटोरी में रखा होता है। इस कटोरी को डबरा कहते हैं। कॉफ़ी को ऊँचाई से दोनों के बीच बार-बार उड़ेला जाता है, ताकि वह ठंडी हो और उसमें झाग आ जाए। बहुत-से तमिल और कन्नड़ घरों में जब तक यह उड़ेलना शुरू न हो, दिन शुरू ही नहीं होता।

sec.h: कॉफ़ी से नींद क्यों भागती है
sec.t:
कॉफ़ी का कैफ़ीन दिमाग़ के एक रसायन, एडेनोसिन, का रास्ता रोक देता है। वह दिमाग़ की [[cell|कोशिकाओं]] पर बने एडेनोसिन के [[receptor|रिसेप्टरों]], यानी उसके तालों, में ख़ुद जाकर बैठ जाता है। एडेनोसिन दिन भर में धीरे-धीरे जमा होता है और हमें नींद का एहसास कराता है।

sec.h: दुनिया की सबसे बड़ी कॉफ़ी की केतली
sec.t: 1800 के दशक से ब्राज़ील दुनिया में सबसे ज़्यादा कॉफ़ी उगा रहा है, और उसके बाद [[@vietnam|वियतनाम]] आता है। अमेरिका में लगभग कोई कॉफ़ी नहीं उगती, बस [[@hawaii-islands|हवाई]] और [[@puerto-rico|प्यूर्टो रिको]] में थोड़ी-सी, पर अमेरिकी लोग कॉफ़ी ख़ूब पीते हैं। बहुत-से लोग कहते हैं कि [[@american-revolution|बोस्टन टी पार्टी]] के बाद, जब चाय अंग्रेज़ों से जुड़ गई, तो कॉफ़ी देशभक्ति का पेय बन गई।

text: प्याज़ की [[cell|कोशिकाओं]] में गंधक वाले कुछ रसायन होते हैं, और अलग-अलग ख़ानों में ऐसे [[enzyme|एंज़ाइम]] भी होते हैं जो इन रसायनों को बदल सकते हैं। छुरी जब कोशिकाओं को तोड़ती है, तो दोनों आपस में मिल जाते हैं। कुछ ही सेकंड में एक के बाद एक कई क्रियाएँ होती हैं और syn-propanethial-S-oxide नाम की एक गैस बन जाती है।

यह गैस चॉपिंग बोर्ड से उठकर हवा में तैरने लगती है। आँखों तक पहुँचते ही यह उनकी सतह की [[@nervous-system|नसों]] को छेड़ देती है, और वे इसे किसी चुभने वाली चीज़ की तरह महसूस करती हैं। दिमाग़ वही करता है जो धूल या धुएँ के लिए करता है: [[@eyes-tears|आँसू की ग्रंथियों]] को हुक्म देता है कि आँखें धोकर साफ़ कर दो। तो तुम रो पड़ते हो, जबकि तुम ज़रा भी उदास नहीं होते।

facts: चीन के साथ दो सबसे बड़े उत्पादकों में से एक (2024 में भारत पहले नंबर पर)
एशिया की सबसे बड़ी प्याज़ मंडी

sec.t:
प्याज़ रसोइयों को रुलाने के लिए नहीं बना। आँसू वाली गैस उसकी सुरक्षा का हिस्सा है। कोई जानवर या कीड़ा कच्चे प्याज़ में दाँत गड़ाए, तो उसका मुँह तीखी, चुभती चीज़ से भर जाता है, और कई बाक़ी प्याज़ को छोड़कर चले जाते हैं।

जब तक कोशिकाएँ साबुत रहती हैं, ये रसायन बेकार पड़े रहते हैं। इसीलिए शेल्फ़ पर रखा साबुत प्याज़ आँखों में पानी नहीं लाता। क्रिया तभी शुरू होती है जब प्याज़ को चोट लगे, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे सेब काटने पर उसका [[@food-science-apples-brown|भूरा पड़ना]] शुरू होता है। इसके बारे में [[@apples|सेब भूरा क्यों होता है]] में पढ़ो।

बहुत समय तक वैज्ञानिक मानते थे कि प्याज़ के सारे तीखे रसायन एक ही एंज़ाइम बनाता है। 2002 में जापान की एक खाद्य कंपनी के शोधकर्ताओं ने एक दूसरा एंज़ाइम ढूँढा, जो ख़ास तौर पर आँसू वाली गैस बनाता है। उन्होंने उसका नाम लैक्रिमेटरी फ़ैक्टर सिंथेज़ रखा। "लैक्रिमा" लैटिन में आँसू को कहते हैं।

इस खोज से बिना आँसू वाले प्याज़ का रास्ता खुला। तब से पौधे तैयार करने वालों ने ऐसे प्याज़ उगाए हैं जो बहुत कम आँसू-गैस बनाते हैं, और कुछ अब अमेरिका की दुकानों में बिकते हैं। कुछ लोग अपने तेज़ [[@taste-smell-link|स्वाद]] की वजह से पुराने तीखे प्याज़ ही पसंद करते हैं। लहसुन, लीक और चाइव्स भी इसी पौधा-परिवार के हैं और लगभग यही रसायन इस्तेमाल करते हैं। पर [[@ginger-garlic|लहसुन]] आँसू-गैस बहुत कम बनाता है, इसीलिए उसे छीलते समय रोना नहीं आता।

गैस हवा से होकर जाती है, इसलिए जो भी चीज़ उसे आँखों से दूर रखे, वह काम की है। खुली खिड़की के पास या रसोई के एग्ज़ॉस्ट फ़ैन के नीचे काटो तो गैस उड़ जाती है। चश्मे जैसे गॉगल्स तो उसे पूरी तरह रोक देते हैं, भले ही रसोई में तुम थोड़े अजीब दिखो।

प्याज़ को आधे घंटे फ़्रिज में रखने से क्रियाएँ धीमी हो जाती हैं। तेज़ छुरी कोशिकाओं को कुचलने की बजाय साफ़ काटती है। जड़ वाला सिरा सबसे आख़िर में काटो, क्योंकि रसायन वहाँ ज़्यादा भरे होते हैं। तुम्हारा [[@blinking|पलक झपकाना]] और आँसू बहाना अपना काम ही कर रहे हैं: तुम्हारी [[@eyes-see|आँखों]] की नाज़ुक सतह की रक्षा।

जब प्याज़ को तेल में धीमी आँच पर पकाया जाता है, तो तीखे रसायन टूट जाते हैं या भाप बनकर उड़ जाते हैं, और प्याज़ नरम, सुनहरा और मीठा हो जाता है। गर्मी प्याज़ की शक्कर की लंबी ज़ंजीरों को भी छोटी, ज़्यादा मीठी शक्करों में तोड़ देती है, जो फिर भूरी होने लगती हैं। इसीलिए इतने सारे भारतीय पकवानों का पहला क़दम होता है प्याज़ को सुनहरा होने तक भूनना। इसके बारे में [[@cooking-science|पकाने से क्या होता है]] में पढ़ो।
